payroll_run.title: Payroll 3 — The Payroll Run
payroll_run.desc: The pay run in ZhiftERP: the Payroll Entry lifecycle across five stations; the six-line pre-run checklist and the records close; generation — company, posting date, period, filters, Get Employees, Create Salary Slips, the one-run rule; the draft review's three checks (headcount reconciliation, register comparison, spot-check slips); submission, the accrual Journal Entry, the posting tie before payment, and the custody sweep; the bank entry and payment under the separation with the three-way total; the five-line close; and the correction and off-cycle lanes.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — The run: one document, one procedure
lessons.html:
This module runs the payroll. Modules 1 and 2 built the records; this module executes them monthly through one doctype — the Payroll Entry — wrapped in one written procedure. The module covers: the Payroll Entry form and its lifecycle, the pre-run checklist, the draft review, submission and the posting, the payment, the post-run close, and corrections.

What the Payroll Entry is. One Payroll Entry document is one pay run for one period: it selects the employees, generates their Salary Slips as drafts, submits them in bulk, books the accrual Journal Entry, and anchors the bank payment. Everything the run does hangs off this one document, which is what makes the run auditable: the month's payroll has one reference, and every slip, posting, and payment traces to it.

The lifecycle, previewed. The run moves through five stations, and the module's chapters follow them:

1. Prepare — the records brought current before the run touches anything: joiners assigned, leavers dated, leave recorded, changes previewed (Chapter 2).
2. Generate — the Payroll Entry created, employees pulled, draft slips created (Chapter 3).
3. Review — the drafts read against the checks before anything submits: the headcount reconciliation, the register comparison, the spot-checks (Chapter 4).
4. Submit and post — the slips submitted, the accrual Journal Entry booked, the posting tied (Chapter 5).
5. Pay and close — the bank payment under the separation, the register filed, the custody sweep (Chapter 6).

The timing frame. The run is a calendar event with dated stations — for a 25th payday, a working shape is: records closed by the 20th, drafts generated and reviewed the 21st-22nd, submitted the 23rd, paid the 25th, closed by the 27th with the remittance calendar (module 2) taking over. The exact dates are the business's; the order is this module's and does not vary: nothing submits before the review, nothing pays before the posting ties, and nothing is closed before the register files.

The one-operator risk, named. The run concentrates power: the person who prepares it should not be the person who releases its money (module 2's separation, applied to salaries), and the review stations exist precisely so that errors — and anything worse — must pass a read that is not the preparer's own. The checklist is not bureaucracy; it is the run's audit face.

Module contents. Chapters 2-6 walk the five stations. Chapter 7: corrections and the off-cycle cases. Chapter 8: HealthTrade's first three runs. Chapter 9: review and the law.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — Station 1: the pre-run checklist
lessons.html:
The run computes from the records as they stand at generation. Station 1 brings the records current, on a written checklist, closed by a stated date (the records-close date — the 20th in the working shape). Walk the lines.

1. Joiners. Every employee who started this period: Employee record verified (module 1, Chapter 2 — the seven fields, the attachments), Salary Structure Assignment created with Base from the offer letter and the slab attached, and the joiner's slip previewed against the letter (module 1, Chapter 7). A joiner missing any of these is excluded from the run and paid on the correction lane — worse for everyone; hence the checklist.

2. Leavers. Every exit this period: Status and Relieving Date set on the Employee record, so the final slip prorates to the date and later runs exclude them (module 7 completes the exit computation — settlements, encashments; this line is the run's dependency).

3. Pay changes. Every approved rise or adjustment effective this period: recorded as a new assignment from the effective date (module 1's supersession rule), previewed. The approval evidence attached — the run executes decisions; module 6 governs them.

4. Leave and absence. Approved leave-without-pay and unapproved absences recorded in the leave machinery by the records-close date — payment-days proration (module 1, Chapter 6) reads them at generation. The month's LWP list is printed for Station 3's spot-checks: the reviewer must know which slips should show reduced days.

5. Variable pay inputs. Overtime, bonuses, commissions, and one-off deductions for the period, entered through module 5's machinery (Additional Salary records) by the close date, each with its approval. The run picks them up automatically; late entries become correction-lane traffic.

6. The standing records unchanged. A one-line confirmation: no component, structure, or slab changed since last run — or, where one did, the change ran module 8's discipline (previewed per affected structure, logged). The run should never be the place a structural change is discovered.

The close line. At the records-close date the checklist is signed — every line confirmed or its exception named — and the inputs freeze: what arrives after the close waits for next month or takes the correction lane deliberately. The freeze is what makes Station 3's review meaningful; a review of moving records reviews nothing.

Practical rule: the checklist is a standing document with the month's date, kept in the payroll folder beside the register it will produce. Six lines, most of them one word — done — and the run's quality is decided here, before the Payroll Entry exists.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — Station 2: generating the run
lessons.html:
Open Payroll Entry (awesome bar) > New. Walk the form, top to bottom.

1. Company and Posting Date. The employing entity, and the date the accrual will book to — month-end for the standard monthly cycle, so the cost lands in the month it belongs to (the Accounts track's period discipline).

2. Payroll Frequency and the period. Monthly, with the Start Date and End Date defining the period the slips compute — the payment-days engine counts working days inside these dates.

3. The selection filters. The run can scope by Branch, Department, Designation, or company-wide. The standing design: one run per company per period, unscoped, so no employee can fall between two partial runs — scoped runs are for the deliberate exception (a branch on a different cycle), recorded as a design decision, not improvised monthly.

4. The payable and payment defaults. The payroll payable account (the net-pay liability the accrual credits — module 2, Chapter 6's map) and the payment account/mode defaults the bank entry will use. Set once, verified at the first run's posting read, untouched after.

5. Get Employees. The button pulls every employee matching the filters with an active assignment in the period into the document's employee table. Read the table before going further:

• The count. Against the expectation: last month's count + joiners − leavers. This is the first sighting of the headcount reconciliation (Station 3 formalises it); a surprise here is cheaper than a surprise in the drafts.
• The absences from the list. A missing employee means a missing or lapsed assignment — back to Station 1's checklist, fix the record, Get Employees again. The run never proceeds around a missing person "to be fixed later".

6. Create Salary Slips. The button generates one draft Salary Slip per listed employee, each computed from that employee's assignment, structure, components, slab, and payment days — modules 1 and 2 executing in bulk. Drafts, deliberately: nothing has posted, nothing has paid, everything is readable and correctable. Station 3 now owns them.

The generation log line. One line in the payroll log: period, filter scope (company-wide), employee count pulled, slips created, date, by whom. The line seems trivial until the month it is not — the run that was generated twice, the scope that was accidentally filtered — and the log is where those diagnoses start.

Practical rule: generate once, after the records close — not "early to see" and again later. A regenerated run must first cancel its earlier drafts cleanly, and two generations in one period is exactly how a stale draft slips through to submission. One close, one generation, one review.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — Station 3: the draft review
lessons.html:
The drafts exist; nothing has posted or paid. Station 3 is the read that stands between computation and money — three checks, in order, evidenced.

Check 1 — the headcount reconciliation. One line of arithmetic, written on the checklist:

last month's paid count + this month's joiners − this month's leavers = this month's draft count.

The joiner and leaver names are listed (Station 1 produced both lists). If the equation does not balance, the difference is named by person before anything else happens — the joiner whose assignment lapsed, the leaver still active, the duplicate. The reconciliation is thirty seconds when clean and the single highest-value control in the run: it is the check that catches the ghost employee, the missed exit, and the double slip, which are payroll's three classic frauds and its three classic accidents alike.

Check 2 — the register comparison. The Salary Register report (module 2, Chapter 8) runs on the draft slips, beside last month's closed register:

1. Column totals first: gross, each statutory column, net — each delta explained by the month's known events (headcount change, rises, variable pay, prorations). A column that moved with no story is a finding.
2. Per-employee movements next: every material change against its document — the rise's new assignment, the LWP's reduced payment days, the Additional Salary record behind a variable line. The Station 1 LWP list is ticked off here: every listed absence visible on its slip, no unlisted reductions.
3. The comparison is before payday by design — module 2 called this read's purpose: an unexplained movement found now is a record fix; found after payment it is a recovery conversation.

Check 3 — the spot-check slips. A small set opened and read line-by-line (module 1, Chapter 7's five reads): every joiner and leaver (their prorations are the month's riskiest arithmetic), one slip per structure, and one random pick. The payment-days field on each against the calendar and the LWP list; the statutory lines against module 2's expectations.

The review's evidence. The checklist's Station 3 block records: the reconciliation equation with its numbers, the register-comparison exceptions and their explanations, the spot-checked names, reviewer, date. Where the reviewer is a second person (the separation's stronger form — recommended wherever staffing allows), their sign-off is the block's last line.

Fixes found here. Every finding is fixed in the records (module 1's rule): the assignment corrected, the leave record completed, the component repaired — then the affected draft slip is regenerated (delete the draft, recreate from the Payroll Entry, or correct-and-recompute per the document's tooling) and the relevant check re-run. Never edit a draft's figures by hand: a hand-edited draft passes review and lies to it at the same time.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — Station 4: submit and the posting tie
lessons.html:
The drafts are reviewed and signed. Station 4 converts them into payroll.

Submitting the slips. On the Payroll Entry, Submit Salary Slips submits every draft in the run. What submission does, precisely:

1. Each Salary Slip becomes a submitted document — docstatus 1, immutable, correctable only by cancel/amend (the platform's document law, now protecting payroll).
2. The run books its accrual Journal Entry: the posting module 2 Chapter 6 mapped — salary expenses debited by component with each employee's Payroll Cost Center, the custody payables credited (PAYE, pension, NHF at the run's withheld totals), the net-pay liability credited at the run's net total. The Payroll Entry links to the Journal Entry it created; large sites may see the posting consolidated per the entry's settings — the map is the same.

The posting tie — immediately, before payment.

1. Open the accrual Journal Entry from the Payroll Entry.
2. View > Accounting Ledger. Read the rows against the register's column totals: gross to the expense lines (cost centers present on every P&L row), each custody column to its payable credit, net to the payable-to-employees credit.
3. Tie confirmed, one line on the checklist: posting tied to register, [date], [initials]. A mismatch at this station is a wiring fault (module 2's diagnosis) — and it is found with the money still unmoved, which is the entire reason the tie sits before Station 5 rather than at month-end.

The point of no return, stated plainly. Submission is the run's commitment: the slips are now the month's payroll of record, the books carry the cost, and the remittance obligations (module 2) now exist at these amounts. Corrections after this point follow Chapter 7's lanes — cancel/amend on documents, never quiet edits. This is why Stations 1-3 are written procedure: everything cheap happens before this button.

The custody sweep. With the accrual booked, the custody amounts are known and owed: the sweep to the tax-reserve bank account (the Accounts track's reserve discipline; module 2, Chapter 7's funding step) is prepared now — the withheld totals moved from the operating account to the reserve, so remittance day draws on money that was set aside at the moment it became custody, not scraped together at the deadline.

Practical rule: Station 4 is one sitting — submit, tie, sweep-prepared, checklist signed — scheduled on its calendar date (the 23rd in the working shape). Splitting it across days is how a run ends up submitted-but-untied over a weekend, which is precisely the state the procedure exists to prevent.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — Station 5: payment and the close
lessons.html:
The slips are submitted, the posting is tied, the reserve is funded. Station 5 moves the money and closes the month.

The bank entry. From the Payroll Entry, Make Bank Entry generates the payment posting: the net-pay liability debited, the salary bank account credited — the accrual's counterpart, dated the payment date. Where the business pays through a bank upload, the payment file is produced from the run's data (employee, bank name, account number — module 1 Chapter 2's verified fields — and net amount), and the file's total must equal the run's net total and the bank entry's amount: one figure, three places, agreeing before release.

The separation, executed. Module 2's rule 1 of bank governance, applied to the month's largest single payment:

1. The payroll operator prepares: the bank entry drafted, the payment file produced, the three-way total written on the checklist.
2. The release authority — a different person, holding the bank mandate — reviews the file against the checklist's evidence (the reconciliation equation, the tied posting, the totals) and releases.
3. Neither person can pay alone; the file the releaser sees is the file the checklist describes. This is the station where the ghost-employee fraud dies even if every earlier check somehow missed it: the releaser's list has names on it, and names are checkable.

Payment exceptions. The bounced credit (a wrong account number that survived verification): the bank's return is matched to its employee, the Employee record corrected under the bank-detail custody rule (written instruction, filed), and the individual re-payment made and referenced to the run — the exception documented on the run's log, never handled by an off-books transfer.

The close, on the checklist's last block.

1. The register filed: the month's Salary Register produced from the submitted slips — the closed record every schedule derives from (module 2, Chapter 8's one-register rule) — into the payroll folder.
2. The custody sweep executed: the reserve transfer released (prepared at Station 4), the reserve now holding the month's statutory money.
3. The remittance calendar armed: module 2, Chapter 7 takes over — schedules derived, payments prepared, the pension window counting from the payment date just made.
4. The payslip delivery triggered — module 4's territory, referenced here as the close's communication line.
5. The checklist signed and filed beside the register: the run's complete evidence — six station blocks, every check's numbers, every exception's story — one document an auditor reads top to bottom.

Practical rule: the month is closed when the checklist says so, not when the money moved. A paid-but-unclosed run leaves the register unfiled, the sweep unexecuted, and the remittance clock running silently — the three loose ends that surface as module 2's four custody stories.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — Corrections and the off-cycle cases
lessons.html:
Errors found after submission, and payments that cannot wait for the cycle. Both run on lanes, never on improvisation.

The correction lane — a submitted slip is wrong.

1. Found before payment (between Stations 4 and 5): cancel the slip (and its share of the posting per the document's cancel behaviour), fix the record at fault (module 1's rule — the assignment, the component, the leave record), regenerate and resubmit the slip, re-tie the posting, and note the correction on the checklist. The run pays right the first time; the cost was an hour.
2. Found after payment: the money has moved, so the correction is two-sided. Underpayment: the difference is paid promptly — an off-cycle payment referenced to the corrected slip, because the employee should never wait a month for the business's error. Overpayment: the recovery is agreed with the employee in writing (a deduction on the next slip through module 5's machinery, or a repayment plan for large amounts — the employee's cash flow is real, and the law and the relationship both prefer agreed recovery), documented, and executed through the records. In both directions: the record at fault is fixed so the error does not recur, and the incident line names the cause — a correction whose cause is not named will be performed again.

The off-cycle payment — money outside the run. The lawful cases: the final settlement that cannot wait for month-end (module 7's territory), the correction payment above, the advance under module 5's advance machinery. The rules that keep off-cycle honest:

1. Every off-cycle payment has a document — a slip, a settlement computation, an advance record — never a bare bank transfer with a story.
2. Off-cycle payments post to the same accounts the map names, addressed the same way.
3. The month's register plus its off-cycle documents together equal the month's payroll cost — the tie extends to cover them, and the checklist's close block lists them.

What has no lane, stated once. Editing a submitted slip's figures, paying "outside the system" to fix a system error, netting an overpayment against an underpayment across two employees, and holding an error quiet until next month all share one property: they make the records disagree with the money. Every lane above exists so that the records and the money never disagree — which is the whole track in one sentence.

Practical rule: corrections are logged in the payroll log with cause, lane, and dates — and the quarterly read of that log (the sysadmin track's cause-read discipline) is where recurring causes get their upstream fix: the checklist line added, the verification tightened, the record governed harder.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Case study: HealthTrade's first three runs
lessons.html:
The procedure, run three times — each month exercising a different station's value. (Thirty staff, three structures, the module 2 statutory build live.)

Run one — the full walk. Records close on the 20th: the checklist's six lines signed, one exception named (a variable-pay input arriving on the 21st — held to next month, deliberately, and the submitter told why: the freeze is real). Generation on the 21st: Get Employees pulls thirty; Create Salary Slips makes thirty drafts. Station 3: the reconciliation equation reads 0 prior + 30 loaded − 0 = 30 (the go-live month's form); the draft register is compared against the old spreadsheet's final month — every delta explained, most by the corrections module 1's previews had already made; spot-checks on one slip per structure. Submit on the 23rd; the posting tie reads clean against the wiring the module 2 preview verified. Payment on the 25th: the file's total, the bank entry, and the register's net agree — the MD releases against the checklist. Close on the 26th: register filed, sweep executed, remittance calendar armed. The checklist files as the run's one-document story.

Run two — Station 3 earns its keep. The records close clean; thirty-one drafts generate (one joiner). The register comparison flags one movement with no story: a warehouse assistant's net up — no rise on file, no variable line. The spot-check opens the slip: payment days show a full month, but Station 1's LWP list has him down for four unpaid days — the leave record was never entered. The fix runs the lane: the leave record completed in the leave machinery, the draft regenerated, the comparison re-run clean, and the incident line names the cause: the branch supervisor's leave submissions were arriving by message, not through the system. The upstream fix lands the same week — leave enters through the leave machinery by the records-close date, and the checklist's line 4 now says so explicitly. Found at draft: a record fix. Found after payday: a recovery conversation with a man who had already spent it.

Run three — the mid-month joiner. A pharmacist joins on the 16th. Station 1 processes her fully: record verified, assignment from the 16th with Base from the letter, slab attached, preview read with her offer letter open — the letter quotes the monthly package; the preview shows the payment-days fraction for a 16th start, and the number is explained to her at onboarding, before the first payday, with the arithmetic on paper. The run generates thirty-two drafts; her slip's payment-days figure is a spot-check line; payday brings no query from her because the answer preceded the question. The payroll log's note beside the three checklists: three runs, three different catches, one procedure — the stations are earning their dates.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common mistakes & the third law
lessons.html:
The run's recurring failures, then the review list.

Pattern 1 — the run without a close. Symptom: inputs trickling in until the hour of submission; every review reviewing a moving target; "one more change" as a standing state. Cause: no records-close date (Chapter 2). Fix: the close line on the calendar, the freeze enforced, late inputs to next month or the deliberate correction lane — and the review made meaningful by the stillness it reads.

Pattern 2 — the skipped reconciliation. Symptom: the ghost employee paid for months; the leaver paid after leaving; the duplicate slip; each discovered by accident or audit. Cause: the headcount equation never written (Chapter 4). Fix: the one-line arithmetic on every checklist, differences named by person before anything proceeds — thirty seconds against payroll's three classic failures.

Pattern 3 — the hand-edited draft. Symptom: a draft's figures adjusted directly to "fix" a finding; the review passing a slip whose records disagree with it; the same error recomputing next month. Cause: fixes made downstream of the fault (Chapter 4). Fix: the rule — records fixed, drafts regenerated, checks re-run; the draft is a computation's output, never an editing surface.

Pattern 4 — pay before the tie. Symptom: money released while the posting is unread; wiring faults discovered at month-end with the cash already gone; the register and the ledger telling different stories. Cause: Station 4's order broken (Chapter 5). Fix: the sequence made absolute — submit, tie, then payment — with the tie's line on the checklist as the releaser's precondition.

Pattern 5 — the single pair of hands. Symptom: one person prepares, reviews, and releases the month's largest payment; every control self-attested. Cause: the separation not applied to payroll (Chapters 1, 6). Fix: the release authority distinct from the preparer, reviewing the file against the checklist's evidence — and where staffing allows, the Station 3 reviewer distinct too.

Pattern 6 — the invisible off-cycle. Symptom: transfers outside the run with verbal explanations; the month's payroll cost no longer equal to its documents; recoveries that were never agreed and payments never referenced. Cause: off-cycle handled without its lane (Chapter 7). Fix: every off-cycle payment on a document, posted on the map, listed in the close block — the register plus its off-cycle documents equalling the month, always.

The review list. Before the quiz, confirm you can: name the five stations and the timing frame; run the six-line pre-run checklist and defend the records close; walk the Payroll Entry form — company, posting date, period, filters, Get Employees, Create Salary Slips — and state the one-run rule; execute the three draft-review checks with their evidence; state what submission does, run the posting tie, and place the custody sweep; execute the payment under the separation with the three-way total and run the five-line close; and route corrections and off-cycle payments on their lanes.

The third law: the run is a procedure — records closed, drafts reconciled and read, posting tied before payment, payment separated from preparation, and the month closed on the checklist that proves it. Module 4 covers the payslip: the employee's side of everything this run produced.

payslips.title: Payroll 4 — Payslips, Communication & Confidentiality
payslips.desc: The payslip in ZhiftERP: the slip as the employee's statement and the publisher-not-author custody; the slip's anatomy including working days versus payment days and the YTD block; the print format with the specimen and second-reader disciplines; Payroll Settings' delivery machinery — Email Salary Slip to Employee, Encrypt Salary Slips in Emails — with its dependencies and the one-person test; the payday calendar and the five-step query procedure; the access matrix and employee self-service; and the six confidentiality working rules.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — The slip: the employee's statement
lessons.html:
This module covers the payslip from the employee's side: the Salary Slip's anatomy, its print form, the delivery machinery in Payroll Settings, the payday communication routine, the query procedure, and the confidentiality rules that govern all of it.

What the slip is. The Salary Slip is the employee's statement of one period's pay: what was earned, what was deducted and why, what was paid. It is the payroll function's only regular product that every employee reads — the register, the postings, and the schedules serve the business and the authorities; the slip serves the person. Its quality standard is therefore different: a slip is good when the employee can follow it — every line named in plain words (module 1's component-naming rule yielding returns), every change from last month explainable, the net matching the bank credit to the naira.

Why the slip earns a module. Three reasons, each practical:

1. Trust is the payroll function's product. Staff who understand their slips query less, suspect less, and accept corrections faster — the module's routines are cheaper than the confusion they replace.
2. The slip is evidence. Loan applications, visa applications, disputes, and statutory queries all ask for payslips; the slip's completeness and its delivery trail matter beyond payday.
3. The slip is the confidentiality frontier. Every slip is one person's private financial information, produced in bulk monthly — the delivery and access machinery is where payroll's confidentiality is kept or lost (Chapters 6-7).

The slip's place in the pipeline. The run (module 3) generates and submits the slips; this module takes over at Station 5's close: the delivery is triggered after payment, so no employee reads a slip for money that has not arrived — a small ordering rule that prevents a standing category of payday anxiety.

The custody note. The slip's content is computed by the records — modules 1 and 2 own every figure on it; nothing in this module changes a number. This module owns the slip's presentation, delivery, explanation, and protection: the payroll operator as the statement's publisher, not its author.

Module contents. Chapter 2: the Salary Slip's anatomy, field by field. Chapter 3: the print form. Chapter 4: the delivery machinery — Payroll Settings. Chapter 5: the payday routine and the query procedure. Chapter 6: access and self-service. Chapter 7: confidentiality. Chapter 8: the HealthTrade case. Chapter 9: review and the law.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — Reading the Salary Slip, field by field
lessons.html:
Open any submitted Salary Slip. Walk it as the employee will — top to bottom — because Chapter 5's query procedure is this walk performed aloud.

1. The header. Employee, employee number, designation, department/branch, the period (start and end dates), and the company. The header answers "whose pay, for when, from whom" — and on a multi-company site the company line is the legal employer, which matters on every slip used as evidence.

2. Working days and payment days. The period's working days (from the employee's Holiday List) beside the days being paid. Equal in a full month; different when proration ran — the joiner, the leaver, the LWP (module 1, Chapter 6). These two numbers explain more payday queries than every other field combined: your payment days were 22 of 26 — four unpaid leave days, here is the leave record is a complete answer.

3. The Earnings table. One row per earning component: name and amount. The reading rules: component names in plain words (the register's naming rule), amounts as computed — the prorated figure where Depends on Payment Days ran, the formula's result where a formula ran, the Additional Salary line where variable pay landed (module 5's rows appear here, named for what they are: Overtime — March).

4. The Deductions table. One row per deduction: PAYE, pension (employee share), NHF where it applies, loan and advance recoveries (module 5), any agreed one-off. The employer pension share appears per module 2's configuration — visible, clearly not reducing net — so the employee sees the full contribution their fund receives.

5. The totals block. Gross pay (earnings summed), total deduction, net pay — and the rounded total where rounding is configured. Net is the number the bank credit must match to the naira; any slip-to-bank difference is a payment exception (module 3, Chapter 6), never a shrug.

6. The year-to-date figures. Where the slip layout carries them: cumulative gross, tax, and deductions for the payroll year — the fields that make the slip useful for annual tax reconciliation and that answer "how much tax have I paid this year" without a register extract.

7. The references. The slip links its Payroll Entry and its assignment lineage — the operator's trail, not printed for the employee, but the reason any slip's every figure can be traced to a record in under a minute (Chapter 5 uses this).

Practical rule: once per year, read one slip end-to-end with a new employee as part of onboarding — ten minutes that converts the slip from a mysterious PDF into a readable statement, and cuts the year's queries at the source.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — The slip's print form
lessons.html:
The slip's print is what employees keep, banks request, and embassies file. It is governed by the sysadmin track's print machinery, applied here.

The format. The Salary Slip's print format shows: the letterhead (the business's legal identity — the Letter Head doctype, so every slip is identifiably from its employer), the Chapter 2 anatomy in reading order, and nothing hard-typed (the sysadmin track's rule: identity from the letterhead, figures from the document — the bank-details-fossil failure applies to slips exactly as to invoices).

The format decisions, made once.

1. One default format, signed off as the specimen (the sysadmin track's specimen discipline): a sample slip printed to PDF, read by the payroll operator and one non-payroll reader — the second reader is the purpose: the format is good when someone who does not run payroll can follow it — and filed as the standard.
2. The employer pension share's presentation confirmed: visible, labelled as the employer's contribution, unmistakably not a deduction from the employee.
3. The YTD block's inclusion decided — recommended on, for the evidence uses above.
4. Changes to the format are governed events through the change lane (the sysadmin track, module 5): test-site preview, sign-off, the specimen replaced, the change date logged — because a format change alters every slip printed from that day, and slips in circulation are compared across months.

The PDF discipline. The slip is delivered as PDF (Chapter 4); the PDF is the product. After any format, letterhead, or platform change, one slip prints to PDF and is read against the specimen — the smoke test's print step (the sysadmin track, module 5) with the slip on its checklist, because a payroll month's broken PDFs are discovered by thirty employees at once, which is the loudest possible way to find a print fault.

Reprints and copies. Employees lose slips and request copies — routinely, and the routine is governed:

1. A reprint is generated from the submitted slip — the document of record; there is never a "corrected reprint" that differs from it (a correction is a document event, module 3 Chapter 7, and produces its own amended record).
2. Copies are delivered to the employee themselves through the same confidential channels as originals (Chapter 4) — a slip copy handed to a third party (the relative at the gate, the caller claiming to be the bank) is a confidentiality breach with a helpful face; third-party requests route through the employee's own written consent, every time.
3. Bulk historical requests (the loan application wanting six months) are one request, six PDFs, one delivery — logged like any export of salary data (Chapter 7).

Practical rule: keep the specimen PDF beside the register in the payroll folder. "Does this month's slip still look like the specimen" is a thirty-second check that catches the format drift no one else will report politely.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — The delivery machinery: Payroll Settings
lessons.html:
Open Payroll Settings (awesome bar). This settings page governs how slips reach employees, and its fields are walked and recorded like every settings page in the programme (the sysadmin track's settings-walk rule).

1. Email Salary Slip to Employee. Ticked, the system emails each employee their own slip on submission — one mail, one recipient, one attachment, automatically. This flag is the delivery machinery's centre, and it carries three dependencies verified before it is trusted:

• The Employee records carry email addresses — the preferred email field on each Employee, verified at joining (module 1, Chapter 2's walk extends here) and treated as governed contact data: changes on the employee's own instruction.
• The sending identity is the business's — the Email Account and domain identity the sysadmin track built (its module 6); slips from a personal mailbox fail every test that module set.
• The Email Queue is watched — slip delivery rides the queue; the payday delivery is a known monthly spike, and its absence is a finding (the sysadmin track's volume read, with payroll now depending on it).

2. Encrypt Salary Slips in Emails. Ticked, the attached PDF is password-protected, with the password format defined beside the flag (built from fields the employee knows). The recommendation is on: an emailed slip travels through mail systems and sits in inboxes the business does not control; encryption means a forwarded, misdelivered, or exposed mail does not expose the salary. The password scheme is told to every employee once, at onboarding, and never in the same email as a slip.

3. The posting and computation flags. Payroll Settings also carries run-behaviour settings (payment-days calculation basis, rounding, the include-holidays choice that changes what "working days" means on every slip — set once with the accountant, recorded, and never changed casually because it changes every proration in the company) — walked, decided, and written into the settings record per the standing rule. Their detail belongs to modules 1 and 3; this chapter's point is that they live on this page and the page is owned.

The delivery run, as a procedure.

1. Payment confirmed (module 3, Station 5) — delivery follows money.
2. Slips submitted → the emails queue automatically (flag 1), encrypted (flag 2).
3. The operator checks the Email Queue: the payday spike present, errors zero, bounces handled — a bounced slip email is a wrong address, corrected on the Employee record under the contact-data rule and resent individually.
4. Employees without email (the genuine cases): the printed-slip lane — sealed, handed to the employee personally, never left on desks or given to supervisors to distribute (Chapter 7's rules; a slip in a supervisor's hands is a breach with a workflow).
5. One log line: period, delivered count by channel, bounces and their fixes.

Practical rule: test the machinery on one person first — the operator's own slip, emailed and opened, password and all — every time any link in the chain changes (address source, sending identity, encryption scheme, format). The one-person test is the difference between a delivery run and thirty simultaneous surprises.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — The payday routine and the query procedure
lessons.html:
Payday produces questions on a schedule. The routine answers them the same way every month, and the query procedure turns each question into a five-minute documented read.

The payday communication calendar. Three dated lines, published to staff once and kept:

1. Payment date — when the credit lands (module 3's Station 5 date).
2. Slip delivery — same day or next, after payment confirms (Chapter 4's ordering rule).
3. The query window — the stated channel and period for payslip questions (a named contact, the first week after payday). A published window is not a limit on rights; it is a promise of attention — queries inside it get same-week answers, and the batching keeps the operator's month workable.

The query procedure. Every query runs the same five steps, and the first four are Chapter 2's walk performed with the person:

1. Open the slip together (in person, on a call, or by reply) and read the line in question.
2. Trace it to its record — the payment-days figure to the calendar and the leave record; the earning to the assignment's base and the structure's formula; the deduction to the component's rule and, for statutory lines, the accountant's table (module 2's division of authority: the operator explains how it computed; rate-policy questions route to the accountant); the variable line to its Additional Salary record and approval.
3. State the answer in the employee's terms — "your net changed because four unpaid leave days reduced payment days from 26 to 22; here is the leave record" — the record shown, not just cited.
4. If the record is wrong, say so and run the lane — module 3 Chapter 7's correction paths, with the employee told the timeline. A query that finds a real error is the procedure succeeding, not failing; the worst outcome is the defensive non-answer that converts a question into a grievance.
5. Log the query — one line: who, what line, the answer, any correction opened. The log's quarterly read (the cause-read discipline) finds the patterns: five queries about the same allowance is a naming or communication fix; three about proration is an onboarding-explanation fix.

The standing answers. Most queries are four questions wearing different slips, and the operator keeps their answers rehearsed: why did my net change (proration, LWP, a new or ended deduction, a tax-table change — the month-on-month register comparison already knows, because module 3's Station 3 explained every movement before payday); what is this deduction (the component's rule and its page); why is my tax this amount (the slab walk, with the accountant behind it); when does my rise show (the assignment's From Date and the run it lands in).

Practical rule: the register comparison's explanations (module 3) are written before payday — which means every "why did my net change" already has its answer on file. The routine is fast because the run did the work; payday queries are retrieval, not investigation.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — Access and self-service
lessons.html:
Who can open a Salary Slip, and how employees reach their own. The sysadmin track's permission machinery, applied to payroll's most personal documents.

The access matrix. Salary Slip access is role-permissioned to the shortest possible list:

1. The payroll operator — full access: the function's work.
2. The review/release authority and the accountant — read access: the separation's reviewers and the numbers' policy owner.
3. The employee — their own slips only, through self-service (below).
4. Nobody else by default. Supervisors do not read their teams' slips; HR-adjacent roles do not browse; the curiosity read is not a use case (the sysadmin track's phrasing, verbatim, because the rule is the same). Where a business role genuinely needs payroll data (a branch P&L question), the answer is an aggregate from the register's grouping — totals by cost center — not slip access.

Employee self-service. The platform's employee-facing access lets each employee see their own records — their slips among them — under their own login:

1. The employee's User account links to their Employee record (the linkage is the fence: the permission machinery scopes their view to documents that are theirs).
2. Their slip list shows their own history — which quietly retires the copy-request routine of Chapter 3 for every enrolled employee: the six-months-for-the-bank request becomes self-service.
3. Enrolment follows the sysadmin track's user rules: real named accounts, the joiner/leaver procedures covering them, and the leaver's access ending on the date (their slips remain in the business's records; their login to anything ends).

The verification read. Access is confirmed, not assumed — twice:

1. At setup: log in as a test employee account and confirm the view: own slips visible, any other employee's invisible, the payroll doctypes' lists scoped. The sysadmin track's diagnosis path (test-as-the-role) applied to the most sensitive scope on the site.
2. At the quarterly recertification: the payroll access list read by name — who holds operator access, who holds read access, and whether each still holds the job that justifies it. Payroll access rides the standing recertification; it is named here because its list must be the shortest one reviewed.

The export permission, restated. Module 2's register rule reaches the slip doctype too: export rights on payroll doctypes sit in the sysadmin matrix as consequential grants — the slip list exported is the register by another door, and the door count includes it.

Practical rule: when anyone asks for slip access, the first question is "what read do you actually need?" — the answer is almost always an aggregate, a specific documented disclosure (Chapter 7), or the employee's own consent path, and almost never a standing grant. Grants are for functions, not questions.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — Confidentiality: the working rules
lessons.html:
Payroll confidentiality fails through small workflows, not dramatic breaches. This chapter is the working rules — each one a failure mode with its fence.

1. One mail, one recipient. Slips are emailed individually by the machinery (Chapter 4) — never manually batched. The manual batch's failure is the address field: thirty attachments in one mail, or thirty recipients on one slip, is the payroll equivalent of the reply-all disaster, and it has happened at businesses that were sure it would not. The automated one-to-one delivery plus encryption is the fence; if a manual send is ever unavoidable (a bounced-mail resend), it is one mail, one person, the address read twice.

2. Print custody. Printed slips exist sealed and reach the employee's own hands (Chapter 4's printed lane). The failure modes and their fences: slips left at the printer (print at need, collect immediately — the payroll printer habit); slips distributed through supervisors (never — the supervisor reading their team's pay on the way is the predictable outcome); the discarded misprint (shredded, not binned).

3. The spoken layer. Payroll questions are answered to the employee themselves, in private — not across an open office, not to the colleague asking "for" them, not to the spouse on the phone. Identity before content on any remote query: the operator confirms they are speaking to the employee (a call-back to the number on record beats trusting an inbound caller) before any figure is spoken. The social-engineering pattern the sysadmin track named — the convincing voice asking for a reset — arrives in payroll as the convincing voice asking for a salary figure.

4. Third-party disclosures. Banks, landlords, embassies, and courts ask for salary confirmations. The lane: the employee's own written consent names the recipient and the content, the disclosure is made in writing from the business (the employment-confirmation letter with its salary line, or the consented slip copies), and one log line records it. Statutory demands (an authority's lawful request) route through the accountant and the owner — the operator's job is the lane, not the legal judgment.

5. The operator's own conduct. The role reads every salary; the discipline is the professional one, stated plainly at appointment and repeated at the annual review: payroll knowledge is used for payroll work — never in social currency, never in the operator's own negotiations, never as leverage in any direction. The register's confidentiality rules (module 2, Chapter 8) — access-listed exports, business-controlled storage, aggregates in meetings — are this rule's mechanical half.

6. The screen and the desk. The payroll workstation locks when left (the session rules); the register is not open on a screen facing the walkway during payroll week; the payroll folder — digital and physical — sits in access-controlled storage, not the shared drive's open root.

Practical rule: the annual confidentiality read walks these six with everyone who holds payroll access — fifteen minutes, examples included — and each person confirms in writing. The written confirmation is not ceremony: it is what makes the standard enforceable the day someone tests it.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Case study: HealthTrade's payday
lessons.html:
The slip machinery installed and the first payday cycles run. Every chapter appears.

The format and the specimen (Chapters 2-3). The slip's print format is reviewed against Chapter 2's anatomy: component names already read plainly (module 1's naming rule yielding returns), the employer pension line relabelled Employer Pension Contribution after the non-payroll test reader — the warehouse supervisor drafted in for the second-reader test — flags it as "looks like they're deducting it twice." Exactly the catch the second reader exists for. YTD block on. The specimen PDF signs off and files beside the register.

The delivery build (Chapter 4). Payroll Settings walked and recorded: Email Salary Slip to Employee on; Encrypt Salary Slips in Emails on, the password scheme set and told to staff at a five-minute briefing — never in slip emails. The dependencies verified in order: the Employee-record email sweep finds four missing and two stale addresses (fixed on the employees' own instruction); the sending identity is the domain account the sysadmin build moved to; the operator's own slip runs the one-person test — mailed, opened, password works, PDF matches the specimen. Three staff without email addresses take the printed lane: sealed, personal hand-over at the branch, the supervisor-distribution shortcut explicitly declined when offered.

The first delivery (Chapters 4-5). Payment confirms on the 25th; slips deliver the same afternoon. The Email Queue shows the expected thirty-mail spike; one bounce — a typo'd address — is corrected on the record and resent individually. The published calendar goes up: payment the 25th, slips same day, queries to the payroll operator through month-end.

The query window (Chapter 5). Week one brings four queries, each logged: two are the proration question (the run-two LWP case and a new joiner — both answered by the payment-days walk, records shown); one is what is NHF (answered from the applicability page; the pattern noted — the deduction pre-dated anyone explaining it); one finds a real error — a transport allowance missing from one slip, traced to an assignment loaded against the wrong structure at go-live. The correction runs module 3's lane: underpayment paid off-cycle within the week, the assignment corrected, the employee told the timeline on day one. The quarterly query read later turns the NHF question into a one-page "what your deductions mean" note issued with January slips — three queries a month become zero.

The consent lane tested (Chapter 7). Month two, a bank calls "verifying" an employee's salary for a loan. The operator declines the phone disclosure, and the lane runs: the employee signs the consent naming the bank, the confirmation letter issues in writing, one log line. The employee gets their loan; the salary figure never travelled on an inbound phone call. The payroll log's note: the slip machinery ran a full quarter — delivered encrypted, queried through the window, disclosed only on consent — and the register never left the folder.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common mistakes & the fourth law
lessons.html:
The slip layer's recurring failures, then the review list.

Pattern 1 — the unreadable slip. Symptom: cryptic component codes, unexplained figures, a monthly PDF nobody can follow; queries high and trust low. Cause: the slip treated as a system artifact instead of a statement (Chapters 1-3). Fix: plain component names, the anatomy in reading order, the second-reader test on the format, and the onboarding slip-walk that teaches each employee to read their own.

Pattern 2 — the manual batch. Symptom: slips sent by hand in bulk; the month one address field goes wrong, thirty salaries go public. Cause: the delivery machinery unused (Chapters 4, 7). Fix: Email Salary Slip to Employee on, encryption on, the one-mail-one-recipient rule absolute, and manual sends reserved for individual resends with the address read twice.

Pattern 3 — delivery before money. Symptom: slips arriving for salaries not yet credited; payday anxiety manufactured monthly. Cause: the ordering rule unknown (Chapters 1, 4). Fix: delivery triggered at Station 5 after payment confirms — the calendar publishes both dates and keeps them.

Pattern 4 — the defensive non-answer. Symptom: queries met with "the system computed it"; questions hardening into grievances; real errors surviving because no one traced the line. Cause: no query procedure (Chapter 5). Fix: the five steps — open together, trace to the record, answer in their terms, run the lane if wrong, log — and the quarterly read turning query patterns into upstream fixes.

Pattern 5 — the open door. Symptom: supervisors reading team slips, broad roles browsing the slip list, exports in personal drives. Cause: slip access never matrixed (Chapter 6). Fix: the four-line access list, self-service for own-slips, aggregates for business questions, export rights as consequential grants, and the test-as-the-role verification.

Pattern 6 — the helpful disclosure. Symptom: salary figures given to callers, copies to relatives, confirmations without consent — each one a favour, each one a breach. Cause: the third-party lane missing (Chapter 7). Fix: written consent naming recipient and content, written disclosures only, identity-before-content on every remote query, and the log line each time.

The review list. Before the quiz, confirm you can: state what the slip is and the publisher-not-author custody; walk the slip's seven blocks and explain payment days versus working days; govern the print format — specimen, second reader, the reprint and copy rules; operate Payroll Settings' delivery flags with their three dependencies and run the delivery procedure with its one-person test; keep the payday calendar and run the five-step query procedure with the four standing answers; hold the access matrix and self-service rules with their verification reads; and apply the six confidentiality working rules with the annual written confirmation.

The fourth law: the slip is the employee's statement — computed by the records, delivered one-to-one after the money moves, explained on request from the records, and confidential everywhere else. Module 5 covers variable pay: overtime, bonuses, commissions, advances, and the Additional Salary machinery.
