variable_pay.title: Payroll 5 — Variable Pay: Overtime, Bonuses, Commissions & Deductions
variable_pay.desc: Variable pay in ZhiftERP: the four rules and the component-carries-everything design; the Additional Salary doctype field by field — component, amount, payroll date, Overwrite Salary Structure Amount, recurring From/To dates, Deduct Full Tax on Selected Payroll Date; the overtime lane with approved-before-worked and the two control reads; bonuses with the list-drift check and the tax-timing policy; commissions from the system's own sales figures; agreed recoveries on self-terminating schedules; the Employee Advance lifecycle; and loan recovery from the slip with affordability at approval.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — Variable pay enters as documents
lessons.html:
This module covers the pay that changes month to month: overtime, bonuses, commissions, one-off deductions, advances, and loan recoveries. The fixed package is modules 1-2's territory — computed by structures and assignments; variable pay is everything the structure cannot know in advance, and ZhiftERP's answer is one doctype family: variable amounts enter as documents that the run picks up automatically.

The machinery, previewed.

1. Additional Salary — the primary instrument: one record adds one amount (earning or deduction) to one employee's slip for one payroll date, or recurs across a defined span (Chapter 2). Overtime, bonuses, commissions, and one-off deductions all ride it (Chapters 3-5).
2. Employee Advance — money paid ahead of earning or expense, tracked to settlement (Chapter 6).
3. The loan machinery — structured borrowing with a repayment schedule that deducts on the slip (Chapter 7).

The four rules, stated first because every chapter applies them.

1. Approved before the close. Every variable input carries its approval and lands by the records-close date (module 3, Station 1, line 5) — the run picks up what exists at generation; late inputs wait or take the deliberate correction lane. Variable pay is where close discipline is tested monthly, because variable inputs are exactly the ones that arrive late.
2. Computed from evidence. The amount on the document traces to its source: overtime to attendance records and the policy rate, commission to the sales figures, a recovery to its written agreement. The document without its computation is a number with a story, and stories do not survive audits or disputes.
3. Taxed by the flags. The component the document names carries the tax treatment (Is Tax Applicable — module 1's flag; module 2's ruling), and the bonus-month tax mechanics (Chapter 4) are handled by the document's own controls, never by the operator adjusting figures.
4. Recovered by agreement. Every deduction from pay that is not statutory or contractual stands on the employee's written agreement (module 3's overpayment rule, generalised) — the law and the relationship both require it, and the document attaches it.

Where variable pay shows. On the slip, each Additional Salary line appears among earnings or deductions, named by its component (module 4's plain-naming rule: Overtime — March, not ADDL-EARN-07); on the register, the variable columns explain the month-on-month movements module 3's Station 3 reads; on the posting, each amount follows its component's account (module 2's wiring).

Module contents. Chapter 2: the Additional Salary doctype. Chapter 3: overtime. Chapter 4: bonuses and the tax mechanics. Chapter 5: commissions and one-off deductions. Chapter 6: the Employee Advance. Chapter 7: loans. Chapter 8: the HealthTrade case. Chapter 9: review and the law.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — The Additional Salary doctype
lessons.html:
Open Additional Salary (awesome bar) > New. One record, one variable amount, walked field by field.

1. Employee. The recipient. One record per person — a team bonus is a batch of records (imported where volume wants it, under the governed import), never one record "split later".

2. Salary Component. The component this amount rides — an existing, registered component (module 1's register): Overtime, Bonus, Commission, Other Deductions. The component brings everything the amount needs: Earning or Deduction type, the tax flag, the ledger account. This is the design's discipline: the operator never decides an amount's tax or posting at entry — the component decided it once, with the rulings behind it. A variable amount with no fitting component means a new component through the governed lane first, not a near-enough component borrowed.

3. Amount. The figure, from the evidence (each lane's chapter defines its computation). The evidence attaches to this record.

4. Payroll Date. The date that places the amount in a payroll period — the run whose Start/End Dates contain this date picks the record up. Set it inside the intended month, and mind the close: a record dated this month but entered after the records close belongs to the correction lane's decision, not to a quiet backdate.

5. Overwrite Salary Structure Amount. Ticked, the record replaces the structure's own amount for that component this period instead of adding to it. The lawful use is the exception month — the component that normally computes but must be a stated figure this once. The standing caution: overwrite is a per-month override of the package, so it carries approval like a pay change, and its use is rare by design — a component overwritten monthly is a structure that needs fixing (module 1's rule: fix the record, not the output).

6. Is Recurring, From Date, To Date. Ticked, the record applies every period from From to To — the fixed-term item: an acting allowance for a defined cover period, an agreed recovery spread over four months (Chapter 5). The recurrence ends itself at To Date, which is the purpose: a recurring record with honest dates cannot be forgotten on, the way a manual monthly entry can. Open-ended recurring items are a design smell — genuinely permanent amounts belong on the structure or the assignment, not on an Additional Salary that never expires.

7. Deduct Full Tax on Selected Payroll Date. The bonus-month tax control — Chapter 4 owns it; here, know that it exists on this form and defaults off.

The record's lifecycle. Draft → approval evidence attached → submitted before the close → picked up by the run → visible on the slip and register → part of the month's variable-pay register (Chapter 8's list). Submitted records follow document law: corrections by cancel/amend, never edits.

Practical rule: name the record's remarks for the reader — Overtime, 14 hrs @ approved rate, March, per attendance sheet attached — one line that makes the register comparison and every future query self-answering.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — Overtime
lessons.html:
Overtime is the highest-volume variable lane, and the one where evidence discipline pays monthly. The lane, end to end.

1. The policy, written first. Who is overtime-eligible (by role — the policy names the categories), the rate basis (the multiplier on the hourly equivalent, or the flat rate — the accountant and owner set it, the page records it), the authorisation rule (overtime is approved before it is worked, by the named supervisor — the alternative is discovering the month's hours at the close and paying whatever is claimed), and the cap where the business sets one. This page is the lane's law; the operator executes it and никогда — never — arbitrates it: a disputed claim routes to the policy's owner.

2. The evidence. Hours come from records, not recollection: the attendance machinery (the HR track's check-in records) or the signed overtime sheet per the business's practice — countersigned by the approving supervisor, stating date, hours, and the work. The month's sheets close with the records close (module 3, Station 1).

3. The computation. Per employee: approved hours × the policy rate. Computed on the standing sheet (one tab per month: employee, hours, rate source, amount), checked by a second eye where volume is material, and filed — the sheet is the amount's audit trail.

4. The entry. One Additional Salary per employee: the Overtime component (Earning-type; Is Tax Applicable per the accountant's ruling — overtime is generally taxable pay, and the ruling line says so), the computed amount, the payroll date in the month, the sheet attached, submitted before the close.

5. The run picks it up. The slip shows Overtime among earnings; the register's overtime column carries the month's total; Station 3's comparison expects it — the LWP list's twin: the reviewer holds the overtime sheet, so every overtime line on a slip has its sheet line, and no sheet line is missing its slip.

The control reads. Overtime is a standing audit interest because it is discretionary money on repeat, so two reads run monthly and quarterly:

1. The monthly total and its trend (the register column, month on month): overtime that grows quietly is either real workload — a staffing conversation for the owner — or approval drift; the trend read is what forces the question early.
2. The concentration read: the same names every month at the cap is a pattern the policy owner reviews — sustained overtime is either a role sized wrong or a claim habit, and both are management questions the data should raise, not bury.

Practical rule: the approved-before-worked rule is the lane's load-bearing wall. Where it holds, the close is calm and the amounts are routine; where it slips, every month ends in negotiation. Enforce it by routing: unapproved hours go to the policy owner's decision — the operator does not pay them by default, and does not refuse them personally either.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — Bonuses and the tax mechanics
lessons.html:
The bonus lane is simple entry with one technical decision — the tax timing — that this chapter settles properly.

The entry. A bonus is a decision (the owner's or the scheme's), evidenced (the approval memo or the scheme's computation), entered as one Additional Salary per recipient: the Bonus component (Earning; taxable per the standing ruling — bonuses are pay), the amount, the payroll date of the paying month, the approval attached, submitted before the close. Batch bonuses (the year-end round) enter by the governed import, then the register comparison at Station 3 confirms every intended name and no others — the bonus round's classic error is the list drift between the approval memo and the entries, and the comparison is where it dies.

The tax-timing problem, stated plainly. Monthly PAYE is computed by spreading the year's tax over the months (module 2's slab machinery annualises). A large one-off amount in one month disturbs that: taxed as if it were the new normal monthly income, the bonus month can over-withhold; spread thinly, the bonus's tax arrives in pieces across later months. Neither is wrong in law — the annual reconciliation trues it up — but the difference is felt in the employee's bonus-month net, and it should be a decision, not an accident.

The control: Deduct Full Tax on Selected Payroll Date. On the Additional Salary record:

• Ticked: the full tax attributable to this amount is withheld in the bonus month itself — the bonus lands net of its own tax, once, cleanly. The employee's later months are undisturbed. This is the recommended default for material one-off amounts: one month's clarity beats a quarter's confusion.
• Clear: the amount joins taxable income and the slab machinery spreads the effect per its annualisation — acceptable for small amounts where the disturbance is negligible.

The choice is made with the accountant, once, as policy — a line on the ruling page: material bonuses tick the flag; the materiality threshold stated — and then applied consistently, because two employees' identical bonuses taxed on different timings is a fairness question with the operator's name on it.

The communication step. A bonus month's slip is the month most read all year. Two lines of preparation: the bonus line named plainly (Annual Bonus), and — where the flag was ticked — the payday note or the query-window answer ready: the bonus is shown gross; its tax was withheld in full this month, so nothing further hits later months. Module 4's standing-answers discipline, extended by one entry.

The register's face. The bonus column's month-on-month spike is expected and documented — Station 3's comparison ties it to the approval memo's total, the posting tie carries it to the ledger at the component's account, and the custody sweep grows by the month's extra PAYE. The whole pipeline flexes without a single manual adjustment, which is the machinery working as designed.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — Commissions and one-off deductions
lessons.html:
Two lanes sharing one discipline: the amount is computed from evidence and entered as a document.

Commissions. Commission is earned pay computed from sales results, and its lane runs monthly:

1. The scheme, written: who earns commission, on what figure (invoiced sales, collected sales — the difference is a design decision with cash-flow consequences, decided by the owner and recorded), at what rates and thresholds, measured over what period.
2. The source data, from the system: the sales figures come from ZhiftERP's own reports — the sales analytics by salesperson, or the invoice register filtered per the scheme's measure — for the closed period. The commission computed from the system's figures is a commission nobody argues about twice: the invoice list is the evidence, and a disputed line is settled by opening documents, not by comparing recollections.
3. The computation sheet: per earner — the period's qualifying figure, the scheme's arithmetic, the amount — filed with the scheme's version noted (schemes change; the sheet says which rules computed this month).
4. The entry: one Additional Salary per earner on the Commission component (Earning, taxable per ruling), the sheet attached, before the close. Material commission months take the Chapter 4 tax-flag policy like bonuses do.

One-off deductions. Money taken from pay outside the statutory and structural set — the overpayment recovery (module 3, Chapter 7), the agreed damage or shortage recovery where policy provides for it, the staff purchase. The rules are strict because the direction is sensitive:

1. Written agreement, always. The employee's signed agreement states the reason, the amount, and the schedule. No agreement, no deduction — a disputed unilateral deduction is a legal and trust failure that costs more than any recovery, and the till-shortage case in particular follows the POS track's rule: shortages are investigated and resolved by policy, never quietly netted from wages by default.
2. The document: one Additional Salary on the appropriate Deduction component, agreement attached. A spread recovery uses Is Recurring with From/To dates matching the agreed schedule — four months, four equal deductions, self-terminating (Chapter 2's design yielding returns: the recovery that cannot be forgotten on, and cannot silently continue past its end).
3. The affordability line: the schedule is set so the deduction leaves a livable net — the agreement conversation covers it, and a recovery that strips a month's pay is renegotiated, not enforced. The relationship the payroll function protects is worth more than a faster recovery.
4. The register's trail: each active recovery appears on the variable-pay register with its balance run-down — opening agreed amount, deducted to date, remaining — so "how much is left on mine" is a lookup, not a reconstruction.

Practical rule: both lanes close the same way — the month's computation sheets and agreements filed beside the checklist, each register line traceable to its sheet. Variable pay's audit face is the file, and the file is built monthly or not at all.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — The Employee Advance
lessons.html:
Open Employee Advance (awesome bar) > New. An advance is money paid before it is earned or spent, and this doctype tracks it from payment to settlement — the record that prevents the advance from becoming a quiet loan nobody remembers.

The record's fields. Employee; Purpose (written for the reader — medical emergency advance, field expenses, Akure trip); the Advance Amount; the Advance Account — the employee-advances asset account (money owed to the business; the Accounts track's receivable logic, pointed at staff); and the repayment intent.

The two advance kinds, distinguished at issue.

1. The salary advance — pay ahead of payday, recovered from pay. Settlement: deduction via Additional Salary (one-off or recurring per the agreed schedule — Chapter 5's machinery and its written-agreement rule apply verbatim, the agreement being part of the advance's approval).
2. The expense advance — business money for business spending, settled by the expense claim: the employee's claim documents the spending, the claim settles against the advance, and only an unspent remainder is recovered from pay. The two kinds post and settle differently; conflating them is how "the trip money" becomes a payroll dispute.

The lifecycle, as a procedure.

1. Approval: per the policy — who may approve, up to what amount, how many advances outstanding per person (one is the healthy default). The policy page exists before the first advance does.
2. The record submitted, then the payment: a Payment Entry against the advance, referencing the Employee Advance record — the money leaves through the books, debiting the advance account. Never the bare transfer with the record "to follow".
3. The balance visible: the advance record carries its paid and settled amounts; the advances account's balance is the business's total staff exposure — a standing line on the payroll close.
4. Settlement on schedule: the salary advance's recovery deductions run their course (the slip shows them; the register's run-down tracks the balance); the expense advance's claim arrives by the trip's end per policy.
5. The exception read, monthly: the advances account reconciled by person — every balance ageing normally against its schedule. The stale advance (no recovery running, no claim arriving) is chased the month it stalls, because a stalled advance's difficulty compounds: the six-month-old advance meets module 7's exit chapter as a settlement problem.

The custody note. Advances are business money in personal hands — the approval limits, the one-outstanding default, the through-the-books payment, and the monthly reconciliation are the same custody pattern the programme applies to every till and float. The advance that skips the record is indistinguishable from the advance that was never meant to come back.

Practical rule: at issue, the recovery schedule is written into the same conversation as the money — amount, months, first deduction date — and the recurring Additional Salary is created the same day, dated to start on schedule. An advance issued with its recovery already ticking never becomes the awkward conversation.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — Loans and slip recovery
lessons.html:
Where the business lends beyond the simple advance — larger amounts, longer terms — the loan machinery gives the borrowing a structure: an application, an approved loan record, a repayment schedule, and recovery that lands on the slip automatically. This chapter is the operator's working knowledge of that lane.

The lane's records, in order.

1. The policy first (the standing pattern): who is eligible, maximum amounts (commonly expressed against salary multiples), terms, whether interest applies (many staff-loan policies are interest-free; where interest runs, its treatment is the accountant's ruling), and the approval ladder. The page exists before the first loan.
2. The application: the employee's request on the record — amount, purpose, proposed term — routed to the approval per policy.
3. The loan record: the approved loan with its disbursement and its repayment schedule — the month-by-month plan of instalments the system will recover. Disbursement pays through the books (a Payment Entry against the loan account — a staff-loans asset account, the advances account's bigger sibling).
4. Repay from salary: the flag that connects the loan to payroll — set, each period's instalment appears as a deduction row on the slip automatically, per the schedule, until the balance closes. The operator's monthly involvement is verification, not entry: the loan deductions on the register tie to the schedules, which is a five-minute read on the close.

The operator's reads.

1. At the run: loan rows present for every active borrower, absent for everyone else — the register's loan column against the loans list.
2. Monthly: the loans account reconciled by borrower — balances descending on schedule; the missed instalment (an LWP month where net could not carry it, a schedule error) surfaced and handled per policy, on the record.
3. At events: the borrower's exit meets module 7's settlement chapter — the outstanding balance is a final-settlement line, and for this reason the loans read is monthly and not annual: exits do not schedule themselves around loan terms.

The affordability rule, structural this time. Chapter 5's livable-net line becomes policy arithmetic here: the instalment is sized at approval so that the standing deductions (statutory + loan + any recovery) leave the defined minimum net — checked at approval against the current slip, not discovered at the first short month. A loan whose instalment fails the arithmetic is approved smaller or longer, not hoped through.

The boundary, stated once. The operator runs the machinery — records, schedules, recoveries, reconciliations. Whether to lend, to whom, how much, and what to do about the genuinely distressed borrower are the owner's decisions on the policy's ladder. Payroll executes lending; it never underwrites it.

Practical rule: one page per borrower in the payroll file — loan record, schedule, disbursement reference, recovery history — maintained as deductions run. The page answers the employee's "what's my balance", the accountant's reconciliation, and module 7's settlement, from one place.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Case study: HealthTrade's variable quarter
lessons.html:
The variable-pay machinery installed and one quarter run through it. Every chapter appears.

The lanes built (Chapters 1-2). The components confirmed on the register: Overtime, Bonus, Commission (Earnings, taxable per the accountant's rulings), Other Deductions (Deduction). The overtime policy page is written — eligible roles (warehouse and drivers), the rate basis, approved-before-worked with the branch supervisors named, the monthly cap. The advance policy follows: approval limits, one-outstanding default, through-the-books payment.

Month one — overtime goes live (Chapter 3). The first month's sheets arrive countersigned; the computation sheet prices 62 approved hours across seven staff; seven Additional Salary records enter before the close, sheets attached. Station 3's reviewer holds the sheet beside the register: every overtime line matched, one slip carrying overtime for a name not on the sheet — traced in minutes to a record dated into the wrong month (a February entry meant for March; the Payroll Date field's lesson taught live). Cancelled, re-dated, clean.

Month two — the commission and the advance (Chapters 5-6). The sales commission scheme's first cycle: the qualifying figures pulled from the system's own sales report for the closed period, the computation sheet filed with the scheme version noted, three earners entered on the Commission component. The same month, a driver's medical emergency takes the advance lane: approved within the policy limit, the Employee Advance record submitted, the Payment Entry referenced, and — per the issue-day rule — the recovery agreed and created in the same sitting: a recurring Additional Salary, four equal monthly deductions, From/To dates set, self-terminating. His slip shows the recovery line from the following month; the register's run-down tracks the balance without anyone remembering anything.

Month three — the bonus round (Chapter 4). A mid-year performance bonus for eleven staff. The approval memo's list imports under the governed procedure; Station 3's comparison ties the register's bonus column to the memo's total and catches one name on the memo missing from the entries — the import's silent dropped row, restored before submission (the list-drift error, dying where it is supposed to). The tax decision runs the policy line: the amounts are material, Deduct Full Tax on Selected Payroll Date is ticked on all eleven, and the payday note goes out with the slips: the bonus shows gross, its tax fully withheld this month. Two queries arrive in the window; both are answered by the note's own sentence, records shown.

The quarter's file. Three months of variable-pay registers, each line traceable: overtime sheets, the commission computation with its scheme version, the advance's agreement and run-down, the bonus memo and its tax-policy line. The close checklist's line 5 signed all three months. The payroll log's note: the variable quarter produced not one number without a document — and not one payday argument.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common mistakes & the fifth law
lessons.html:
The variable-pay layer's recurring failures, then the review list.

Pattern 1 — the verbal variable. Symptom: overtime and bonuses arriving as messages and recollections; amounts negotiated at the close; the register carrying numbers with stories. Cause: the document rule unenforced (Chapters 1-2). Fix: every variable amount as an Additional Salary with its evidence attached and its approval on record, entered before the close — no document, no pay, said kindly and held firmly.

Pattern 2 — the borrowed component. Symptom: a commission entered on the Bonus component "because it was there"; tax and posting following the wrong rulings; the register's columns lying by category. Cause: the component-carries-everything design ignored (Chapter 2). Fix: the fitting component or the governed lane for a new one — the operator never decides tax or posting at entry.

Pattern 3 — the immortal recurring record. Symptom: an acting allowance still paying a year after the cover ended; a recovery that ran past its agreed total. Cause: recurring records without honest To Dates (Chapters 2, 5). Fix: From/To dates matching the written term on every recurring record, permanent amounts moved to structures and assignments, and the monthly register read confirming every recurring line still inside its dates.

Pattern 4 — the accidental bonus tax. Symptom: bonus-month nets that surprise everyone — over-withheld or under-withheld by accident; two identical bonuses taxed on different timings. Cause: Deduct Full Tax left to chance per entry (Chapter 4). Fix: the policy line with the accountant — materiality threshold, flag treatment — applied consistently, with the payday note ready.

Pattern 5 — the unilateral deduction. Symptom: shortages and damages netted from wages by default; disputes that outcost the recoveries; trust damage that outlasts both. Cause: the written-agreement rule skipped (Chapter 5). Fix: no agreement, no deduction — the policy route for shortages, the signed schedule for recoveries, the affordability line respected, the register's run-down visible.

Pattern 6 — the evaporating advance. Symptom: transfers to staff outside the books; balances nobody tracks; the exit that discovers a two-year-old "advance" with no paper. Cause: the Employee Advance lane bypassed (Chapter 6). Fix: the record before the money, the Payment Entry referenced, the recovery created on issue day, and the monthly by-person reconciliation of the advances account chasing the stale the month it stalls.

The review list. Before the quiz, confirm you can: state the four rules and the component-carries-everything design; walk the Additional Salary form — component, amount, payroll date, Overwrite, recurring dates, the tax flag — and its lifecycle; run the overtime lane from policy to sheet to entry with its two control reads; enter a bonus round with the list-drift check and the Deduct Full Tax policy; compute a commission from the system's own sales figures and run an agreed recovery on a self-terminating schedule; operate the Employee Advance lifecycle with the two kinds distinguished and the monthly reconciliation; and verify loan recoveries against their schedules with the affordability arithmetic at approval.

The fifth law: variable pay enters as documents — approved before the close, computed from evidence, taxed by the component's flags and the stated policy, and recovered only by written agreement on a schedule that ends itself. Module 6 governs the pay decisions themselves: reviews, rises, and the movement record.

pay_reviews.title: Payroll 6 — Increments, Reviews & Pay Governance
pay_reviews.desc: Pay-change governance in ZhiftERP: the decision/execution split and the operator's procedural refusal; the approval matrix with the four-element evidence standard and the letter as anchor; same-day execution of the single change with preview and movement line; the arrears lane — honest From Dates, the sheet's arithmetic, the Arrears component entry, history standing; promotions via the Employee Promotion record with the silent-difference flag; the annual round's timetable, batch import, and both-ways verification; the movement record and the deciders' reads; and the boundary routing questions.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — Pay changes: decisions executed as records
lessons.html:
This module governs pay changes: who decides them, how they enter the system, how late decisions pay their arrears, how the annual round runs as a batch, and how the movement record keeps every change explained. The machinery is module 1's — the new-assignment rule; this module builds the governance around it.

The frame. A pay change has two halves, and the custody split (module 1) assigns each:

1. The decision — whether, whom, how much, from when. This belongs to management: the owner, the approval matrix (Chapter 2). The payroll operator holds no vote and gives no opinion on amounts; what the operator holds is the data the deciders need (Chapter 6's reads) and the refusal that keeps the lane honest: no approved decision, no record.
2. The execution — the decision entered as records that compute it: the new Salary Structure Assignment (Chapter 3), the arrears document where the decision came late (Chapter 4), the preview, the run. This is the operator's craft, and its standard is exactness: the record says what the decision said — amount, date, person — nothing more, nothing rounded, nothing "while we're at it".

Why governance earns a module. Pay changes are where payroll's discipline is tested by pressure, because every change has an interested party and a deadline:

• The undocumented rise — promised in a corridor, entered from a message — is the classic dispute seed: two people remember two amounts.
• The backdated decision handled casually — history edited, or arrears guessed — breaks the register's honesty in both directions.
• The unexplained movement — a base that changed with no decision on file — is the register comparison's most serious finding, because it is either an error or the thing errors are blamed on.

The module's design makes every change carry its decision like every posting carries its document — the same document-rule, applied to the most sensitive numbers in the business.

The change kinds, previewed. The rise (base up, same package) — Chapter 3. The late decision (effective before it was entered) — Chapter 4's arrears. The promotion (role and package change together) — Chapter 5. The annual round (many decisions, one batch) — Chapter 5. The structure-level change (the package itself redesigned) — Chapter 7's boundary with module 8.

Module contents. Chapter 2: the approval matrix. Chapter 3: executing the single change. Chapter 4: arrears. Chapter 5: promotions and the annual round. Chapter 6: the movement record and the deciders' reads. Chapter 7: the boundaries. Chapter 8: the HealthTrade review. Chapter 9: review and the law.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — The approval matrix
lessons.html:
Before any change enters, the business writes who may decide what. The matrix is one page, and the operator enforces it by routing — the same enforcement pattern as every policy in the track.

The matrix's rows. Per change kind, the deciding authority and the evidence the operator requires:

1. Individual rise inside the annual budget — the approving manager per the business's ladder (branch manager proposes, owner approves is the small-business standard), evidenced by the signed increment letter or the approval on the review record.
2. Off-cycle rise (outside the round) — a higher bar by design: the owner's approval regardless of amount, because off-cycle changes are where exceptions breed. The matrix says so plainly, and the operator routes accordingly.
3. Promotion — the role decision (HR/owner) plus its pay decision, both evidenced (Chapter 5).
4. The annual round — the batch's total approved by the owner against the budget line, then each name per the ladder (Chapter 5).
5. Structure redesign — the owner and the accountant together, because the B/H/T split moves statutory amounts (module 2's dependency, resurfacing).

The evidence standard. Every decision reaching the operator carries: who (the named employee), what (the new base, or the new structure and base), from when (the effective date, explicit), and whose approval (the signature or the recorded approval per the matrix). A message that says "increase Tunde's pay" fails on three of four counts, and the operator's reply is the standard, not the execution: send the letter with the amount and effective date, and it enters same day. The refusal is procedural, kind, and absolute — the operator who executes vague instructions inherits their disputes.

The letter as the anchor document. The increment or promotion letter — addressed to the employee, stating the new terms and the effective date, signed per the matrix — is the change's anchor: it is what the employee agreed to, what the assignment must match, and what settles every future "but I was told" in one look. The operator files it attached to the assignment it produces (Chapter 3), which closes the loop: every assignment traceable to its letter, every letter to its assignment.

Confidential handling, restated. Decisions in flight are the most sensitive traffic payroll carries — the round's list before it is announced, the individual rise before its letter. Module 4's confidentiality rules apply with the volume turned up: the decisions folder access-controlled, no lists in open channels, and the operator's conduct rule (payroll knowledge is never social currency) at its strictest exactly here, because a leaked round is a trust failure across the whole staff at once.

Practical rule: the matrix page is agreed once with the owner and re-confirmed at the annual review. Its value is the pressure it absorbs on the operator's behalf: "the matrix requires the owner's approval for off-cycle changes" is a sentence that ends arguments the operator should never have to win personally.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — Executing the single change
lessons.html:
The approved decision arrives with its letter. Execution is one procedure, run the same way every time.

The procedure.

1. Verify the decision: the four elements present (who, what, from when, whose approval), the approval matching the matrix, the letter in hand.
2. Create the new Salary Structure Assignment: the employee, the structure (unchanged for a plain rise; the new one for a package move), the new Base exactly as the letter states, the From Date exactly the letter's effective date, the Income Tax Slab carried, the letter attached to the record. Module 1's supersession rule executes itself: the new assignment governs from its date; the old one stands as history, untouched.
3. Preview: the changed employee's slip previewed (module 1, Chapter 7) — the new base flowing through the percentages, the statutory lines moving with it (pension on the new B/H/T; PAYE at the new taxable level — the change's full consequence visible before it pays). The preview against the letter is the execution's proof: the letter's package arithmetic and the slip agree.
4. Log the movement: one line in the movement record (Chapter 6): employee, old base → new base, effective date, letter reference, approver, entered by, entered on.
5. The run applies it: the next run whose period contains the From Date computes on the new assignment — no run-side action needed. Where the From Date is mid-month, the period splits correctly by the platform's computation; the preview shows exactly how, and the split's arithmetic joins the payday standing answers for that employee.

The timing cases.

• Decided ahead: the letter dated the 20th, effective the 1st of next month — the assignment enters now with its future From Date, and the change waits correctly. Enter decisions when they arrive; the From Date does the scheduling.
• Decided in-month: effective the 1st, entered the 12th, run generated the 21st — inside the same period, the run computes it fully; only the records-close matters (a decision entered after the close waits or takes the deliberate lane, module 3's rule).
• Decided late: effective before the current period — the assignment enters with its honest past From Date and the already-paid months' difference becomes arrears: Chapter 4's lane. What never happens: the From Date moved forward "to keep it simple". The date is the decision's; simplicity is the arrears lane's job.

The employee's side. The letter told them the terms; the first changed slip shows them computed. Where the change lands mid-month or with arrears, the two-line explanation is prepared before payday (module 4's standing-answer discipline): what the letter said, what this slip shows, why they match. A rise that arrives with a confusing slip wastes the goodwill it bought.

Practical rule: same-day execution as the service standard — a complete decision entered the day it arrives. The lane's speed is what keeps decisions flowing through it rather than around it, exactly as with the sysadmin track's change lane.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — Arrears: the late decision's lane
lessons.html:
A decision effective in the past — the review that concluded in March effective January, the letter signed after the effective date. The months between were paid on the old base, correctly, by the records as they stood. The difference owed is arrears, and it has a lane.

The two halves of the late change.

1. The go-forward half: the new assignment with its honest past From Date (Chapter 3's rule — the date is the decision's). From the current run onward, pay computes on the new base. The past runs' slips are not reopened: they were correct when computed, they are submitted documents, and the arrears lane exists precisely so history can stand.
2. The arrears half: the already-paid months' shortfall, computed and paid as its own document.

The arrears computation. On the standing sheet, per affected employee:

1. Per month from the effective date to the last paid run: the components as they would have computed on the new base, minus as they did compute — the earnings difference. For percentage structures this is arithmetic: the base delta flowed through the package's rates; a proration month (a January joiner with a January-effective rise) prorates the delta identically.
2. Sum the months. The sheet shows its working — months, deltas, total — and files with the letter.
3. The statutory consequence rides automatically: arrears are taxable pay in the month paid, and the pension family recomputes on the arrears' B/H/T share — the sheet notes the components' split so the entry (next step) carries it correctly.

The entry. One Additional Salary per employee (module 5's machinery — this is its most important standing use): an Arrears component (Earning-type, taxable, wired to the salary expense family — created once through the governed lane, on the register), the sheet's total, the current payroll date, the sheet and letter attached. Material arrears take the Deduct Full Tax policy line like bonuses do (module 5, Chapter 4) — same logic, same consistency rule. Where the split matters to statutory computation (the pension share of arrears), the entry follows the accountant's ruling on how the arrears components are structured — one line or split lines — decided once, on the page.

The slip and the explanation. The arrears month's slip shows the regular pay on the new base plus the arrears line — a large slip that generates the year's most predictable query. The answer is prepared: the letter (effective January), the sheet (three months' difference, here is the arithmetic), the tax note where the flag was ticked. Shown once, understood permanently.

The movement record's entry. The late change logs like any change (Chapter 3), plus the arrears reference: the sheet, the Additional Salary record, the month paid. The register comparison for the arrears month expects the spike and holds its documents.

Practical rule: arrears exist because decisions were slow, not because payroll was wrong — and the quarterly movement read (Chapter 6) counts them. A business paying arrears every quarter has a decision-timing problem upstream; the count is how the operator hands that fact to the owner as data instead of complaint.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — Promotions and the annual round
lessons.html:
Two composite changes: the promotion (role and pay together) and the annual round (many changes, one batch).

The promotion. A promotion changes the job and the pay, and the records change in order:

1. The role half: the Employee Promotion record — the platform's document for the event: employee, promotion date, and the property changes it applies (the new Designation, Department or Branch where they move, and related fields). Submitted, it updates the Employee record's properties from the date and stands as the event's document — the role history readable later as a chain of promotion records rather than a mystery of edited fields.
2. The pay half: the new Salary Structure Assignment per Chapter 3 — commonly a structure move (Branch Retail Staff → Management) with the new base, from the same effective date, the promotion letter anchoring both halves.
3. The consequence walk: a structure move changes the package's shape — different components, different percentages — so the preview is read with extra care: the new package against the letter, the statutory lines on the new B/H/T, and where the old package carried items the new one does not (an allowance that ends with the old role), the letter must have said so — the operator flags the silent difference back to the decider before entering, because the employee will find it on the slip if nobody found it before.

The annual round. The yearly review executes many decisions at once, and the batch has its own procedure:

1. The list, approved: the round's schedule — every name, current base, new base, effective date — approved as a total against the budget by the owner, then per name per the matrix. The list is the batch's anchor document.
2. The batch entry: the assignments created from the list — individually at small scale, by the governed import at volume (the sysadmin track's six steps; the import's dropped-row risk answered by the next step).
3. The batch verification — the list tied both ways: every name on the list has its new assignment (none dropped), and every new assignment this cycle is on the list (none invented). The assignment list filtered by the round's From Date is the read; ten minutes that catches both failure directions.
4. Previews by structure plus spot names, the letters issued and attached, the movement record batch-logged.
5. The round's first run: Station 3's register comparison expects a broad movement and holds the list — every base delta on the register matching the list's delta, the month's one big explanation already written.

The round's confidentiality window. Between the list's approval and the letters' issue, the round is the business's most sensitive document — Chapter 2's rules at maximum: the list lives in the controlled folder, discussions happen in private, and the operator's answer to every corridor question is the same: letters come from management on the date they announce.

Practical rule: the round runs on a published internal timetable — decisions closed, letters issued, effective date, first changed payday — agreed with the owner so the round lands inside one payroll cycle. A round that straggles across months manufactures arrears (Chapter 4) out of pure scheduling.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — The movement record and the deciders' reads
lessons.html:
Governance needs memory and measurement: the movement record remembers every change; the reads give the deciders their data. Both are the operator's products.

The movement record. One running register — a line per change, from Chapters 3-5's logging steps: date entered, employee, kind (rise / promotion / arrears / round), old base → new base, effective date, letter reference, approver. The record's uses:

1. The audit answer: any base's history reconstructed in one filter — every value it has held, each with its decision. The assignment list holds the same truth record-by-record (module 1: assignments are never edited, so the chain is complete); the movement record is that chain with its governance columns, readable by a human in order.
2. The reconciliation: quarterly, the movement record ties to the assignment list — every new assignment has its movement line and its letter; a naked assignment (no line, no letter) is the register comparison's most serious finding, investigated as module 8's audit chapter directs.
3. The arrears count (Chapter 4's quarterly read) and the off-cycle count — both handed to the owner as decision-timing data.

The deciders' reads. The operator prepares these for the review cycle — aggregates and structured data, produced from the system, confidentiality rules riding along:

1. The pay register: the assignment list by structure — who is on what package at what base (module 1's standing view), the round's working document.
2. The consistency read: per structure or role family, the base spread — lowest, highest, median — read as aggregates for the deciders to see outliers and compression before the round, not after a grievance. The read surfaces the question (two people, one role, widely different bases); the answer — history, performance, market — is management's, and the operator presents the data without editorial.
3. The cost line: the salary cost by cost center from the register's grouping, and the round's modelled cost — the list's deltas annualised, with the employer statutory riding (the employer pension share moves with every base; a round's true cost is the package cost, not the base cost — the modelling sheet says so with arithmetic).
4. The budget tie: where the business runs the budget machinery on its salary accounts (the Accounts track's budget module), the round's modelled cost reads against the budget line before approval — the matrix's row 4 assumes this number exists, and the operator is who produces it.

The boundary, held. Every read above is data for deciders. The operator who starts recommending amounts has left their lane and taken sides in every future dispute; the operator who produces clean spreads, true costs, and honest counts is the review cycle's most useful person and nobody's antagonist. The value is the discipline.

Practical rule: the reads are produced on the round's timetable, dated, and filed with the round — the deciders decided on this data. When next year's round asks "what did we know last year", the file answers.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — Boundaries: structure changes and the special cases
lessons.html:
The module's edges: changes that look like pay changes but run other lanes, and the cases that test the rules.

The structure redesign. Changing the package itself — the B/H/T split, a component added or removed for everyone on a structure — is not a pay change; it is a machinery change, and it runs module 8's change discipline: decided by the owner and the accountant together (the split moves pension and tax — module 2's dependency), built as a new or amended structure, previewed per affected structure, and applied by new assignments for the affected employees from the effective date (the supersession rule at batch scale — the old assignments computed the old package honestly and stand). The boundary matters because a redesign entered as "just edit the structure" silently changes history's meaning: the old slips reference a structure that no longer says what it said. Module 8 owns the versioning rules; this chapter's job is routing the case there.

The demotion and the reduction. Pay reductions are legally and personally the heaviest change: they require the employee's agreement to varied terms (the letter is a contract variation, signed by both sides — the owner's process, with advice where needed), and only then execute as records — the new assignment at the reduced base from the agreed date, the movement line noting the kind. The operator's line is unchanged and matters most here: no complete evidenced decision, no record — a reduction entered from an instruction without the agreement is the operator executing a breach.

The temporary change. Acting allowances, temporary responsibility pay, secondment terms — pay that changes for a period. The lane is module 5's: a recurring Additional Salary with honest From/To dates (self-terminating — the acting allowance that outlives the acting is that module's Pattern 3), not a base change that must be remembered and reversed. The base moves only for permanent decisions; the distinction is asked explicitly when the decision arrives: permanent or for a period? — and the answer routes the lane.

The correction masquerading as a change. "His base was entered wrong at go-live" is not a pay change — it is an error correction: evidenced against the offer letter (the anchor document proving what the base should have been), corrected by a new assignment from the discovery date plus the arrears lane for the shortfall (or module 3's agreed-recovery lane for the overpayment), and logged as a correction with its cause. The distinction matters for the record's honesty: corrections count in the incident log's cause read; changes count in the movement record. Blending them hides both signals.

The freeze months. The matrix can declare freeze windows — no changes entering during the close or the round's own processing — and the operator holds them like the records close: arrivals during a freeze queue with their letters and enter the day it lifts, From Dates honest, arrears lane covering any gap. The freeze protects the batch's integrity; the honest dates protect the employees'.

Practical rule: every arriving change gets the routing questions in order — permanent or temporary? individual or structural? decision or correction? — thirty seconds that puts each case on its lane before any record is touched.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Case study: HealthTrade's first annual round
lessons.html:
The governance built, then the round run through it. Every chapter appears.

The matrix and the record (Chapters 2, 6). The one-page matrix is agreed with the MD: branch managers propose, the MD approves; off-cycle changes need the MD regardless; the round approves as a total against the budget line first, names second. The movement record opens with the go-live history back-filled from the offer letters — every current base traceable to its letter from day one. The first quarterly reconciliation runs clean: every assignment has its line and letter.

An off-cycle test (Chapters 2-3). Month two, a branch manager messages: increase Kemi's pay, she's carrying the branch. The operator's reply is the standard: the matrix line quoted, the letter template sent. The MD approves, the letter issues — new base, effective the 1st of the following month — and the execution runs same-day: assignment created, letter attached, preview read against the letter (the pension and PAYE lines moving with the base, shown), movement line logged. Kemi's first changed slip matches her letter to the naira; no query arrives.

The round (Chapter 5). The MD sets the timetable: decisions closed by the 10th, letters the 15th, effective the 1st of the next month, first changed payday inside one cycle. The operator produces the deciders' reads (Chapter 6): the pay register by structure, the consistency spread — which surfaces one genuine outlier: two pharmacists, one role, bases eighteen percent apart, presented as data without editorial; the MD resolves it inside the round — and the modelled cost with the employer pension riding, read against the budget line. Twenty-two rises approve. The batch enters by governed import; the both-ways verification catches nothing missing and one extra — an assignment created in a duplicate import row — cancelled before it computes. Letters issue on the 15th; the confidentiality window holds (one corridor question gets the standing answer).

The arrears case (Chapter 4). Two of the twenty-two were review-committee stragglers: decided in the round but agreed effective two months earlier per their review outcomes. Both run the lane: assignments with honest past From Dates; arrears sheets showing the two months' deltas through the package rates; one Arrears component created through the governed lane and registered; two Additional Salary entries with sheets and letters attached, Deduct Full Tax ticked per the materiality line. The arrears month's register comparison expects both spikes and holds both sheets. Both employees get the prepared walk — letter, sheet, tax note — at delivery; zero disputes.

A promotion (Chapter 5). The Ibadan branch supervisor moves to branch manager: the Employee Promotion record carries the designation change from the date; the assignment moves her from Branch Retail Staff to Management with the new base; the preview walk flags that the Retail structure's meal allowance is absent from Management — the letter had not mentioned it; the operator routes the silent difference back to the MD, who amends the letter (the allowance absorbed into the base) before entry. The slip she receives matches the letter she signed. The quarter's movement read goes to the MD as data: twenty-three changes, two arrears cases — both from decision timing — and the note that next year's round timetable closes decisions ten days earlier.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common mistakes & the sixth law
lessons.html:
The governance layer's recurring failures, then the review list.

Pattern 1 — the corridor rise. Symptom: pay changed from messages and recollections; two people remembering two amounts; the dispute arriving with the first slip. Cause: the evidence standard unenforced (Chapter 2). Fix: the four-element standard (who, what, from when, whose approval) with the letter as anchor, the operator's procedural refusal, and same-day execution keeping the lane faster than the corridor.

Pattern 2 — the moved date. Symptom: effective dates shifted forward "to keep it simple"; employees paid less than decided; the letter and the records disagreeing. Cause: arrears treated as too hard (Chapters 3-4). Fix: the date is the decision's, always — the honest From Date plus the arrears lane, whose sheet makes the hard part arithmetic.

Pattern 3 — the reopened month. Symptom: past slips cancelled and recomputed to apply late decisions; the register's history unstable; the payroll tie broken backward. Cause: the two-halves design unknown (Chapter 4). Fix: history stands — the past was computed correctly by the records as they stood; the new assignment goes forward, the arrears document covers the gap.

Pattern 4 — the naked assignment. Symptom: a base changed with no movement line and no letter; discovered by the reconciliation or the comparison; error and mischief indistinguishable. Cause: the logging step skipped (Chapters 3, 6). Fix: the movement line as part of execution, the quarterly assignment-to-record reconciliation, and the naked assignment treated as the serious finding it is.

Pattern 5 — the straggling round. Symptom: the annual review dribbling across months; arrears manufactured by scheduling; the round's cost never modelled against the budget before approval. Cause: no timetable, no batch procedure (Chapter 5). Fix: the published timetable inside one cycle, the list as anchor, the both-ways batch verification, and the modelled cost — employer statutory riding — read against the budget line before names approve.

Pattern 6 — the operator with opinions. Symptom: the operator recommending amounts, arguing cases, taking sides; every dispute finding the operator inside it. Cause: the boundary abandoned (Chapters 1, 6). Fix: data without editorial — spreads, costs, counts, produced clean and dated — and the decisions left with the matrix's owners; the discipline is the value.

The review list. Before the quiz, confirm you can: state the two halves of a pay change and the operator's refusal; hold the approval matrix with the four-element evidence standard and the letter as anchor; execute the single change same-day with its preview and movement line, across the three timing cases; run the arrears lane — honest From Date, the sheet's arithmetic, the Arrears component entry with the tax policy, history standing; execute a promotion with the Employee Promotion record and the silent-difference flag, and run the annual round on its timetable with the both-ways verification; produce the deciders' reads — register, spread, modelled cost, budget tie — without editorial; and route the boundary cases by the three questions.

The sixth law: a pay change is a decision executed as a record — approved on the matrix, anchored to its letter, effective from its honest date, arrears by document, history standing, and every movement explained by the record. Module 7 covers exits: the final slip, the settlement, and the leaver's payroll close.
