exits_special.title: Payroll 7 — Exits, Full & Final & Special Cases
exits_special.desc: Exits in ZhiftERP: the Relieving Date and Status as the exit's first records and the two payment shapes; the final slip's proration with the five-document preview and the statutory tail; Leave Encashment from policy line to record with the start-of-exit balance confirmation; the settlement sheet's two columns and the Full and Final Statement with the leaver's signature before release; closing loans, advances, and recoveries with the insufficient case's owner-decision lane; the ten-line release checklist including same-day access closure; and the special cases on the one operator's rule.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — The exit: payroll's closing procedure
lessons.html:
This module closes the employment relationship from the payroll side: the exit's records, the final slip's proration, leave encashment, the settlement computation and its document, the closure of loans and advances, the release checklist, and the special cases. The exit is where every earlier module's records are read one last time — and where every earlier shortcut presents its bill.

The exit's shape. An exit is a decision (resignation accepted, contract ended, termination decided — HR's and the owner's territory, with professional advice where the case needs it) executed as records (this module's territory). The custody split holds to the end: the operator computes and documents what the records and the decisions say; the operator decides nothing about the exit itself.

The records that start it. Two fields on the Employee record, set by HR the day the exit is confirmed:

1. Relieving Date — the last day of service. Every computation in this module hangs on it: the final month's proration, the encashment cutoff, the settlement date.
2. Status — moves to Left effective the relieving date, which is what removes the employee from future runs (module 3's Get Employees selects by it — the leaver who keeps getting paid is module 3's Pattern 2, and this field is its fix).

The exit's two payment shapes. The business chooses per case, on the checklist:

1. Inside the final regular run: the relieving date falls in the period; the run prorates the final slip automatically; the settlement items (encashment, recoveries) enter as documents before the close and ride the same run. The default where dates allow — one run, one posting, one payment, all the standing controls applying.
2. The off-cycle settlement: the exit that cannot wait (an immediate departure, a mid-month termination the business chooses to settle at once) — module 3, Chapter 7's off-cycle lane: a documented slip and settlement, posted on the map, listed in the month's close. Off-cycle is the exception with its lane, never the improvised transfer.

What the exit reads from earlier modules. The final computation touches everything: the assignment (the base the last month computes on), the payment-days engine (module 1 — the proration), the statutory set (module 2 — final pay is taxed and pensioned normally), the variable machinery (module 5 — encashment and recoveries enter as documents), the loans and advances registers (module 5's monthly reads deciding whether this exit is routine arithmetic or a recovery problem), and the sysadmin track's leaver procedure (access ending the same day — Chapter 7's cross-track line).

Module contents. Chapter 2: the final slip. Chapter 3: leave encashment. Chapter 4: the settlement computation and its document. Chapter 5: closing loans and advances. Chapter 6: the release checklist. Chapter 7: the special cases. Chapter 8: the HealthTrade exits. Chapter 9: review and the law.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — The final slip
lessons.html:
The leaver's last Salary Slip computes like any other — by the records — with the Relieving Date doing the work.

The proration. The payment-days engine (module 1, Chapter 6) reads the Relieving Date exactly as it reads the Date of Joining in reverse: a relieving date of the 12th gives payment days from the period's start to the 12th; the components with Depends on Payment Days pay their fraction; flat components pay per their flags. No manual arithmetic — the operator's job is verification, not computation:

1. The Employee record's Relieving Date against the accepted resignation or the decision letter — the date is the decision's, entered exactly.
2. The final slip previewed (module 1, Chapter 7's procedure — the exit is a standing preview trigger): payment days against the calendar, each line's fraction sensible, the statutory lines present.

The statutory lines on final pay. Final pay is pay: PAYE computes through the slab on the final taxable income, the pension family computes on the final B/H/T fractions, NHF per its rule — nothing switches off because someone is leaving. Two exit-specific notes for the accountant's page:

• The encashment's tax treatment (Chapter 3) is ruled separately — encashment is its own kind of payment and the ruling says how it taxes.
• The remittance continues past the person: the leaver's final PAYE joins the month's state schedule, their final pension joins their PFA's schedule — the custody chain (module 2) does not care that the employment ended, and the leaver's PFA remittance in particular is the one most often dropped, because the person is gone before the schedule runs. The checklist (Chapter 6) carries the line.

Notice-period mechanics, from the payroll side. The contract's notice terms are HR's to apply; payroll executes the outcome as records:

• Notice worked: the relieving date is the notice's end; the final slip prorates to it. Nothing special.
• Notice paid in lieu: the payment-in-lieu is a settlement item — computed per the contract's terms on the sheet (Chapter 4), entered as a documented earning, taxed per the ruling.
• Notice owed by the employee (leaving short of contractual notice, where the contract provides for recovery): a settlement deduction — with the same written-agreement discipline as every recovery (module 5, Chapter 5): the signed acknowledgment in the exit paperwork, the amount per the contract's formula, on the sheet. Disputed notice recoveries route to the owner; the operator computes both versions and executes the decision.

Practical rule: the final slip is previewed with the exit file open — the resignation/decision letter, the contract's notice terms, the leave balance (Chapter 3), the loans and advances pages (Chapter 5). The exit preview is the one preview that reads five documents, because the final slip is the one slip that answers to all of them.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — Leave encashment
lessons.html:
Where the leave policy pays out unused leave at exit, the platform computes and documents it through its own record.

The prerequisites, in order.

1. The policy line: which leave types encash (annual leave commonly; sick leave commonly not), at what rate basis, and any caps — the HR policy's written line, because encashment is a term of employment, not an operator's kindness.
2. The leave balance, trustworthy: the encashment computes from the leave machinery's balance at the relieving date — allocations minus approved applications (the HR track's records). The exit is where a year of casual leave-keeping presents its bill: a balance nobody maintained becomes a negotiation; a maintained balance is a lookup. The operator verifies the balance with the employee before computing — the leaver confirming their own balance in writing at exit is the lowest-cost dispute prevention in this module.
3. The rate basis, configured: the encashment amount per day derives from the salary structure per the policy's basis (the structure's encashment configuration names the component basis — commonly the Basic-derived daily rate). Set once with the accountant when the structure is built; verified at the first encashment.

The Leave Encashment record. Open Leave Encashment (awesome bar) > New: the employee, the leave type, the leave period, and the balance pulled from the leave records; the record computes encashable days × the per-day rate and, submitted, creates the encashment's entry into the pay machinery — landing on the final slip as its own named line. The record is the encashment's document: the balance, the rate, the arithmetic, and the approval, in one place, attached to the exit file.

The tax line. The encashment's tax treatment is the accountant's ruling (Chapter 2's note): the component that carries encashment holds the ruled flag, and material encashments take the Deduct Full Tax policy consideration like any material one-off (module 5, Chapter 4's consistency rule). The operator's job is the standing one: the ruling on the page, the flag matching it, the plausibility visible on the previewed final slip.

The verification, on the sheet. The settlement sheet (Chapter 4) carries the encashment as a line with its own working: balance [n] days (confirmed by employee, date) × rate [basis] = amount, per Leave Encashment [record] — one line that an auditor, the employee, and next year's operator can each follow without a meeting.

Practical rule: run the balance confirmation at the exit's start, not its end — the resignation acceptance meeting is the moment to hand the employee their leave statement and get the confirmation signed. A balance disputed on the last day delays the settlement; a balance confirmed on the first day makes the encashment arithmetic.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — The settlement computation and its document
lessons.html:
The settlement is the exit's one number — everything owed each way, netted, documented, paid. This chapter is the sheet and the record.

The settlement sheet. One page per leaver, built from the exit file, in two columns:

Owed to the employee:

1. The final slip's net (Chapter 2's prorated month — the sheet references the slip rather than recomputing it).
2. Leave encashment (Chapter 3's line, with its record).
3. Payment in lieu of notice, where the case has it (Chapter 2, per the contract).
4. Any other contractual or agreed items (the owed expense claim, the agreed terminal benefit per policy) — each with its document.

Owed by the employee:

5. Loan balance outstanding (Chapter 5, from the borrower's page).
6. Advance balances unsettled (Chapter 5).
7. Notice recovery, where the case has it (Chapter 2, agreed).
8. Agreed recoveries in flight (module 5's schedules — the remaining balance falls due at exit per the standard agreement wording, which the agreement template says explicitly for exactly this moment).
9. Company property unreturned only as a last resort and only per signed terms — the property checklist (Chapter 6) exists so this line stays empty.

The net, and its sign. The columns net to the settlement figure. Positive: the business pays the leaver. Negative — the recoveries exceed the final pay — Chapter 5's escalation: the shortfall is the owner's decision on the record (repayment agreement, or the write-off through the Accounts track's two-signature lane), never a figure quietly absorbed or informally pursued.

The Full and Final Statement. The platform carries the settlement as its own document — the Full and Final Statement record: the employee, the relieving date, the payables and receivables assembled (the settlement sheet's two columns as structured rows), the asset-return status, and the resulting net. Where the site uses it, the record is the sheet's system form — created at the exit's start, completed as the items confirm, and standing as the settlement's document of record with the sheet's sources attached. Either form — the record, or the signed sheet where the business runs on paper — the requirements are identical: every line documented, the net computed once, and both parties' sign-off on the final figure.

The payment. The settlement pays like every payroll payment: through the books (the final run's payment, or the off-cycle Payment Entry referencing the settlement document), under the separation (preparer and releaser distinct — the leaver's settlement is the payment most worth a second pair of eyes, because it is the one payment with no next month to catch an error), to the verified bank account on the Employee record.

The sign-off. The leaver signs the settlement — the figure, the items, the acknowledgment that it is full and final per its terms (the wording is the owner's/adviser's; the operator ensures the signature exists before release). The signed settlement plus its attached documents is the exit's answer to every future claim, and for this reason the release checklist (Chapter 6) will not pay without it.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — Closing loans, advances, and recoveries
lessons.html:
The leaver's open balances — the module 5 registers, read one last time and closed on documents.

The reads, at exit confirmation. The day the exit is confirmed, three lookups from the standing pages:

1. The loan balance — the borrower's page (module 5, Chapter 7): outstanding principal, schedule position. The monthly reconciliation's payoff is exactly this moment: the balance is a known number, not an investigation.
2. The advance balances — the by-person reconciliation (module 5, Chapter 6): anything unsettled, of either kind (the salary advance mid-recovery; the expense advance awaiting its claim — chased now, because the claim that does not arrive before the settlement becomes a recovery line).
3. The recoveries in flight — active recurring deductions and their remaining balances from the run-down register.

The closure arithmetic. Each balance lands on the settlement sheet's owed-by column at its exit-date figure. The standard agreement wording (module 5's templates) makes the mechanics automatic: outstanding balances fall due at exit and settle from the final entitlements — and for this reason the agreements were written that way at issue, for exactly this day.

The sufficient case. Final entitlements cover the balances: the settlement nets positive, the deductions document on the sheet (and enter the final slip or the settlement record per the payment shape), the loan and advance records close, the pages note the closure. Routine arithmetic.

The insufficient case. The balances exceed the entitlements — the settlement nets negative. The lane, in order:

1. The number is established on the sheet — both columns documented, the shortfall exact. No negotiation happens around a soft number.
2. The owner decides, on the record: a post-exit repayment agreement (schedule, signed — the leaver is now a debtor, and the agreement is what makes the debt collectable), or the write-off through the Accounts track's lane (the two-signature rule, the named approval, the posting to the write-off's account — a shortfall absorbed is an expense, and expenses are decided, not accreted).
3. The operator executes and files: the agreement or the write-off attached to the settlement; the loan/advance records closed with their resolution noted; the incident line where the case exposes a process gap (the loan whose affordability arithmetic was skipped, the advance that stalled unreconciled for months — the cause read feeds module 5's upstream fixes).

The prevention, restated once. This chapter is easy or hard in proportion to module 5's monthly discipline: affordability checked at approval keeps balances proportionate to final entitlements; the monthly by-person reconciliation keeps every balance current and chased; the issue-day recovery rule keeps advances shrinking from day one. The exit that finds a two-year stale advance is not an exit problem — it is twenty-four skipped monthly reads presenting together.

Practical rule: the three lookups happen the day the exit confirms, and their figures go on the sheet the same day — the settlement conversation that starts with known numbers stays a conversation; the one that starts with an investigation becomes a dispute.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — The release checklist
lessons.html:
The settlement releases against a checklist — one page, every line initialled, because the exit is the one payroll event with no next month to catch what was missed.

The checklist, in order.

1. The records: Relieving Date and Status set on the Employee record, matching the decision letter. (The final slip's correctness and the leaver's exclusion from future runs both hang here.)
2. The final slip: previewed with the exit file open (Chapter 2's five-document preview), the proration verified, statutory lines present.
3. The leave balance: confirmed with the employee in writing (Chapter 3's start-of-exit rule), the encashment record created and matching.
4. The balances: loans, advances, recoveries — the three lookups on the sheet at exit-date figures (Chapter 5), closures or the escalation documented.
5. The settlement document: the sheet or the Full and Final Statement complete, every line sourced, the net computed once, the leaver's signature obtained.
6. Company property: the property list cleared — devices, keys, cards, stock in custody per the assets register — signed off by the holder of each item's custody. The property line clears before release so the settlement never becomes the lever (and so Chapter 4's line 9 stays empty).
7. Access, the same day: the sysadmin track's leaver procedure — the User disabled on the relieving date, sessions revoked, the shared-credential rotations where any applied, self-service ended (the slips remain in the records; the login does not). The payroll operator does not perform this line; the payroll operator confirms it happened, because the leaver with live access is the finding both tracks named and neither track wants to own after the fact.
8. The statutory tail: the final month's remittances carry the leaver — the PAYE on the state schedule, the pension to their PFA (Chapter 2's most-dropped line, printed here so it cannot be), the certificates and records retained per the statutory periods.
9. The exit documents issued: the certificate of service and the exit paperwork per policy (HR issues; payroll confirms the settlement's copy is in the file), and the final payslip delivered through the standing confidential channel.
10. The payment released — under the separation, to the verified account, referencing the settlement document.

The file. Everything above lands in one exit file per leaver: the decision letter, the confirmations, the encashment record, the sheet/statement signed, the closures, the property sign-offs, the payment reference. The file is the exit's single answer — to the leaver's future query, the auditor's sample, the authority's question — and it is complete on release day or the release waits.

Practical rule: the checklist is initialled as lines complete, not reconstructed at the end. An exit runs over days and hands; the live checklist is what keeps ten lines across three people from becoming nine lines and a surprise.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — The special cases
lessons.html:
The exits that test the procedure. Each keeps the same machinery and changes the handling.

The immediate termination. A dismissal effective at once: the decision and its process are the owner's, with professional advice — misconduct terminations in particular carry legal requirements that precede any payroll action, and the operator's discipline is to wait for the documented decision: no settlement computes from a corridor account of a dismissal. Once documented: the off-cycle shape (Chapter 1), the settlement per the decision's terms (what is paid and what is withheld in a misconduct case is the decision's content, not the operator's judgment), the checklist unabridged — access closure the same day matters most in exactly this case, and the property and settlement lines proceed in whatever order the decision directs.

Death in service. The hardest case, handled with its weight:

1. The tone: the family's contact runs through the owner/HR, once, with care — payroll's arithmetic never leads the conversation.
2. The machinery: the Employee record closes with the date and the appropriate status; the final computation runs the standard sheet — final pay, encashment, entitlements per policy and any group-life/benefits terms (the accountant and adviser rule the items and their treatment).
3. The payment: to the estate or the named beneficiaries per legal advice — never simply to the account on file, because the account's ownership has legally changed; this is the one settlement where the verified-account rule yields to the adviser's instruction, documented.
4. The balances: outstanding loans and advances in a death case are the owner's decision with advice (policies and group cover often address them); the operator documents the resolution, whatever it is.

The disputed exit. Where the exit itself is contested (the resignation retracted, the termination challenged), payroll freezes at the documented state: the records reflect the last documented decision; computations wait for resolution; interim instructions come from the owner in writing. The operator who executes one side's account of a dispute has joined it.

The abandonment. The employee who stops appearing: HR's process runs first (the contacts, the notices, the contractual abandonment terms); payroll's part is the honest interim — unmarked absence reduces payment days per the standing engine (the records tell the truth while the process runs), and the exit computes on the process's documented conclusion and its effective date.

The retirement. The planned exit at its best: months of notice, the balances wound down on schedule (the loan's term set at approval to clear before the date — module 5's affordability arithmetic, time-shaped), the encashment and entitlements computed without pressure, the pension handover to the PFA confirmed. The retirement checklist is Chapter 6's plus the pension-transition line — and a retirement executed cleanly is the exit procedure's best advertisement to the staff who watched it.

Practical rule: every special case shares one operator's rule — the machinery computes; the decisions come documented from their owners. The cases differ in weight and wording; the discipline does not move.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Case study: two HealthTrade exits
lessons.html:
The procedure run twice — once routine, once hard. Every chapter appears.

Exit one — the resignation, end to end. A Head Office accounts assistant resigns with full contractual notice; the relieving date lands on a month-end (the final-regular-run shape, Chapter 1). Day one: HR sets the Relieving Date and Status; the operator runs the three balance lookups — no loan, no advance, one recovery in flight (a staff purchase, two instalments remaining) — and hands her the leave statement at the acceptance meeting: nine days unused annual leave, confirmed and signed same day (Chapter 3's start-of-exit rule). The Leave Encashment record computes the nine days at the structure's ruled basis; the settlement sheet builds: final month's net (full month — the date is month-end, no proration), plus encashment, minus the recovery's remaining balance (the agreement's falls-due-at-exit wording operating as designed). The Full and Final Statement assembles the columns; she signs on her last day. The checklist walks: property cleared (laptop, keys), access disabled the same evening — confirmed with the sysadmin, initialled, the final slip delivered encrypted, payment released by the MD against the signed statement. The statutory tail runs with the month: her final PAYE on the Lagos schedule, her final pension on her PFA's schedule — the checklist's line 8 ticked with the schedules attached. File closed in eleven lines, zero disputes.

Exit two — the termination with the negative settlement. A driver is dismissed mid-month following the owner's documented disciplinary process (the operator waited for the decision letter — Chapter 7's rule, held under pressure to "just stop his pay"). The off-cycle shape applies. The lookups find the hard fact: a staff loan with a balance exceeding the final entitlements — the final prorated pay plus four days' encashment cover most, not all, of it. The sheet establishes the exact shortfall (Chapter 5's rule: the number first); the MD decides on the record: a post-exit repayment agreement for the shortfall, signed at the settlement meeting, three monthly payments. The settlement statement documents both columns, the net, and the agreement; the checklist runs unabridged — access closed the same day (the case where it matters most), property recovered before the meeting, the statutory tail carried. The incident line does its upstream work: the loan pre-dated the affordability arithmetic (approved in the spreadsheet era at a term the salary could not safely carry), and the cause read's note to the MD closes the loop: every loan approved since the policy page carries the arithmetic; this one taught us why. The payroll log's quarter note: two exits, one easy, one hard — both closed on documents, both answerable from one file each.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common mistakes & the seventh law
lessons.html:
The exit layer's recurring failures, then the review list.

Pattern 1 — the leaver who keeps getting paid. Symptom: salary credits after the last day; the recovery conversation with someone who no longer answers. Cause: Relieving Date and Status not set the day the exit confirmed (Chapters 1-2). Fix: the two fields as the exit's first act, the run's headcount reconciliation naming every leaver (module 3's equation working as designed), and the checklist's line 1.

Pattern 2 — the negotiated balance. Symptom: leave balances and loan figures argued at exit; settlements delayed by investigations; numbers agreed by fatigue. Cause: the registers not maintained monthly (Chapters 3, 5). Fix: the standing reads that make every balance a lookup — and at the exit, the day-one lookups and the start-of-exit leave confirmation, so the settlement conversation opens with known numbers.

Pattern 3 — the settlement without a document. Symptom: a final figure paid from a conversation; no signed statement; the claim arriving a year later with nothing to answer it. Cause: the sheet and sign-off skipped (Chapter 4). Fix: the settlement sheet or Full and Final Statement with every line sourced, the leaver's signature before release, and the checklist refusing payment without it.

Pattern 4 — the lever settlement. Symptom: the settlement withheld to force property returns or concessions beyond its terms; the dispute the withholding creates outcosting the item it chased. Cause: the property line run after release instead of before, or the settlement used as pressure (Chapter 6). Fix: the checklist's order — property clears before release day arrives — and disputes routed to the owner as decisions, not exercised through the operator's timing.

Pattern 5 — the dropped statutory tail. Symptom: the leaver's final pension never reaching their PFA; the query arriving months later from the fund or the person; the remittance schedule missing the name that was "already gone". Cause: the tail unowned (Chapters 2, 6). Fix: the checklist's line 8 — the final month's schedules carrying the leaver, attached to the file — and module 2's schedules derived from the register, which still contains the final slip.

Pattern 6 — the live login. Symptom: the leaver's access working weeks after the exit; the finding both tracks named. Cause: the access line assumed rather than confirmed (Chapter 6). Fix: same-day closure by the sysadmin's procedure, confirmed and initialled on the payroll checklist — two tracks, one line, no gap between them.

The review list. Before the quiz, confirm you can: state the exit's shape, the two fields that start it, and the two payment shapes; verify the final slip's proration with the five-document preview and carry the statutory lines including the tail; run the encashment from policy line to Leave Encashment record with the start-of-exit balance confirmation; build the settlement sheet's two columns, use the Full and Final Statement, and handle both signs of the net; close loans, advances, and recoveries with the insufficient case's owner-decision lane; walk the ten-line release checklist; and handle the special cases on the one operator's rule.

The seventh law: the exit closes on documents — the final slip prorated to the relieving date, the balances read the day the exit confirms, the settlement computed once and signed, the statutory tail carried, and the leaver's access ending the same day. Module 8 closes the track: settings, controls, the payroll year, and the eight laws.

advanced_payroll.title: Payroll 8 — Advanced Payroll: Settings, Controls & Structure
advanced_payroll.desc: The structural close of the Payroll track: the full Payroll Settings walk — payroll basis, unmarked attendance, holidays in working days, rounding, leave balances on slips, posting granularity — recorded with reasons; the control register assembling the track's separations, reconciliations, registers, and calendars; structure versioning with period-boundary scheduling; the payroll year — slab and applicability re-reads, annual PAYE certificates, returns, the year file; the six-question audit answered from one folder; multi-company payroll; the handover and absence tests; and the track's eight laws.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — The structural close
lessons.html:
The final module assembles the function: the Payroll Settings walk completed, the control set gathered, the payroll year's calendar, structure versioning, the audit folder, multi-company payroll, the handover test, and the track's eight laws.

Where the track stands. Modules 1-7 built the machinery and its procedures: the records that compute pay, the statutory layer, the run, the slip, the variable lanes, the change governance, the exit. Each module left behind artifacts — registers, checklists, calendars, policy pages. This module's work is structure: making the collection into a function that runs the same regardless of who runs it — the programme's standing test (the Accounts and Sysadmin tracks each closed on it), now applied to payroll.

The three structural claims, previewed.

1. The settings are written decisions (Chapter 2): every behaviour switch on the Payroll Settings page walked, decided, and recorded — because an unexamined setting is a decision someone made by not making it, computing every slip in the company.
2. The controls are layered, not personal (Chapter 3): the separations, reconciliations, registers, and calendars gathered onto one page — visible as a system, auditable as a system, and survivable as a system.
3. The function is answerable from its folder (Chapters 5-7): the payroll year closes on its calendar, the audit answers from one place, and the handover test proves the operator is replaceable — which is the operator's professional achievement, not their diminishment: the function that depends on its holder is a risk; the function that survives its holder is an asset, and building the second kind is what this certification certifies.

The custody split, one last time. The track's standing division closes where it opened: HR owns who and on what terms; the accountant owns the numbers' policy; the owner owns the decisions; the operator owns the machinery and its evidence — and this module is the machinery's own record: how it is configured, controlled, closed, and handed over. Every chapter that follows produces one more page of that record, and the record's completeness is what Chapters 6 and 7 will test.

Module contents. Chapter 2: the Payroll Settings walk. Chapter 3: the control set. Chapter 4: structure versioning. Chapter 5: the payroll year. Chapter 6: the audit folder. Chapter 7: multi-company payroll and the handover test. Chapter 8: the HealthTrade year close. Chapter 9: the eight laws.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — The Payroll Settings walk
lessons.html:
Open Payroll Settings (awesome bar). Module 4 walked the delivery flags; this chapter completes the page — every field read, decided with its owner, and recorded on the settings page (the sysadmin track's walk rule: the walk is the routine occasion for change; between walks the page is stable).

The computation block — decided with the accountant, because each switch changes every proration in the company.

1. The payroll basis — whether payment days derive from leave records or from attendance marking. The choice matches the business's actual discipline: a business that marks attendance daily can compute from attendance; one that manages by exception computes from leave records (absences entered as leave of the right type). The decision is honest about which records the business genuinely maintains — computing from records nobody keeps produces slips nobody trusts.
2. Unmarked attendance handling — where attendance-based computation runs: what an unmarked day means (present or absent). The default posture and its consequence stated on the page: treating unmarked as absent enforces marking discipline sharply (and shorts the slip of everyone the marking missed); treating it as present is forgiving (and pays the absence the marking missed). Decided knowingly, with the HR track's attendance procedures as the counterpart.
3. Holidays in total working days — whether the denominator counts holidays. The switch changes every daily rate and every proration fraction in the company; it is set once with the accountant, recorded with a worked example on the page (one mid-month joiner computed both ways, so the decision is visible as arithmetic), and never changed casually — a mid-year flip makes two halves of the year prorate differently, which is a finding factory.

The presentation block.

4. Rounded totals — whether net pay rounds. Decided with the accountant (the rounding difference posts per the platform's handling); the slip and the bank file must agree either way.
5. Leave balances on the slip — showing each employee their balance on every slip. Recommended on where the leave records are maintained (module 7's start-of-exit confirmation becomes a formality when every slip has been showing the balance all year); left off where the balances would embarrass the record-keeping — and that condition, written on the page, is its own prompt to fix the records.

The posting block — decided with the accountant.

6. Posting granularity — whether the run's accrual posts per employee or consolidated. Consolidated keeps the General Ledger compact; per-employee makes the ledger itself answer person-level questions (at the cost of volume). The decision follows the business's reading habits — module 2's register-derivations pattern already answers person-level questions from the register, so consolidated is the common default — and the posting-read (module 2, Chapter 6) verifies whichever shape was chosen.
7. The delivery flags — module 4's territory, referenced: email delivery on, encryption on, the password scheme's line.

Practical rule: the settings page's record carries, per field: the value, the decision's owner, the date, and the one-line reason. Fifteen minutes at the walk; the alternative is the reconstruction every unexplained setting eventually demands.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — The control set, assembled
lessons.html:
The track's controls, gathered from their modules onto one page — the payroll function's control register, reviewed annually.

The separations.

1. Preparer never releases — the run's payment and every remittance (modules 2-3).
2. The decision/execution split — no record without its approved, evidenced decision (module 6's matrix; module 5's approvals; module 7's exit decisions).
3. The reviewer distinct from the preparer at Station 3, where staffing allows (module 3).

The reconciliations, by cadence.

• Per run: the headcount equation; the register comparison; the posting tie; the three-way payment total (module 3).
• Monthly: the custody zeros after remittance (module 2); the advances and loans by person (module 5); the delivery log's bounces closed (module 4).
• Quarterly: the movement record to the assignment list — the naked-assignment sweep (module 6); the payroll access recertification riding the sysadmin cycle (module 4); the cause reads — corrections, queries, arrears counts (modules 3-6).
• Annually: the slab and applicability re-reads (module 2); the settings walk (Chapter 2); the control register itself.

The registers. The component register with its rulings (module 1); the applicability page (module 2); the movement record (module 6); the variable-pay register with its run-downs (module 5); the borrower and advance pages (module 5); the exit files (module 7); the settings record (Chapter 2).

The calendars. The run's five stations on their dates (module 3); the remittance calendar with the pension window pinned to the payment date (module 2); the review round's timetable (module 6); the annual lines above.

The control register's use. One page listing every control with its owner, cadence, and evidence location. Three readers use it:

1. The operator — the working map; nothing runs from memory.
2. The reviewer/owner — the oversight view: sampling any control's evidence without asking anyone where it lives.
3. The auditor — Chapter 6's visit starts from this page.

The layering logic, stated once. No single control is trusted alone: the headcount equation catches what the close missed; the register comparison catches what the equation cannot see; the posting tie catches the wiring; the releaser's read catches what every earlier layer somehow passed; the quarterly sweeps catch what the runs normalised. The layers are cheap individually — seconds to minutes — and their value is the property that a failure must pass all of them, which honest errors and dishonest ones alike find hard.

Practical rule: when any control finds nothing for a year, the annual review asks whether it is redundant or working — and the answer is almost always working: the control that finds nothing is usually the control whose existence prevents what it would find. Retire controls rarely and deliberately.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — Structure versioning
lessons.html:
Module 6's Chapter 7 routed the structure redesign here. This chapter is the discipline for changing the pay machinery itself.

What counts as a structural change. Anything that alters how a package computes for everyone on it: the B/H/T split moved, a component added to or removed from a structure, a structure-row formula changed, a component's own formula or flag changed (the tax flag ruling revised, a rate updated on the accountant's table), a new Income Tax Slab at a reform. Individual bases are module 6's lane; the machinery is this one.

The versioning rule. The machinery's history must stay readable: every past slip was computed by the records as they stood, and those records must remain visible as they stood. Hence:

1. Slabs: the module 2 rule verbatim — a new dated slab per reform, the old one never edited, attachment by new assignments.
2. Structures: a material redesign is a new structure version (the amended document or the successor structure, named with its effective period where the change is large enough to warrant it), with the affected employees moved by new assignments from the effective date — the supersession rule at batch scale. The old structure and old assignments stand as the record of what computed the past.
3. Components: flag and formula changes on a shared component change every structure that carries it — the impact list is written before the change (which structures, which employees, which statutory lines move), and where the old and new rules must coexist across a boundary date, the answer is a successor component or the structure-row override, never a component whose meaning silently changed mid-year.

The change procedure (the sysadmin track's eight steps, payroll-shaped).

1. The request written with its decision — owner and accountant together for anything touching the split or the statutory set (module 6's matrix row).
2. The impact list from the registers: structures, headcount, statutory consequences.
3. Built and previewed per affected structure in the test discipline — one slip per structure at a representative base, the plausibility check re-run where tax moved (module 2).
4. The before-change backup and the deployment window per the sysadmin rules.
5. The batch assignments entered and verified both ways (module 6's round procedure re-used).
6. The first run's register comparison expecting exactly the modelled movement — the change's own prediction tested against its result.
7. The registers updated: the component register's rulings, the settings record where a setting moved, the movement record's batch note.
8. The announcement — staff told what changes on their slips and why, before the slip tells them.

Practical rule: schedule structural changes to period boundaries — effective the 1st, entered before the close, live for a whole month's first run. A mid-period structural change makes one month compute under two regimes, which is possible but never worth it when a week's patience buys a clean boundary.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — The payroll year
lessons.html:
The annual cycle — the lines that run once a year, on the calendar, closing one payroll year and opening the next.

The year-end block, in order.

1. The statutory re-reads (module 2's standing lines, scheduled here): the Income Tax Slab confirmed against current law with the accountant — a reform produces the new dated slab, attached by new assignments before the first run of the new year; the applicability page re-confirmed line by line; the threshold watch checked against the year's headcount.
2. The annual tax reconciliation and certificates: each employee's year — taxable income, PAYE withheld — reconciled (the register's YTD columns and the slip's YTD block carrying the figures), and the annual PAYE certificate issued per employee per the authority's requirements: the document the employee's own filing and the authority's cross-check both rely on. The certificates derive from the same closed registers as everything else — one source, one truth — and their issue is a calendar line with an owner and a date.
3. The employer's annual returns: the year's statutory filings per authority (the annual employer declarations that accompany the monthly remittance pattern) — the accountant's filings, prepared from the operator's registers and evidence bundles; the division of authority holding at year-end exactly as monthly.
4. The year's registers closed: the movement record's year read (changes, arrears count, off-cycle count — the decision-timing data to the owner); the variable-pay year totals; the loans and advances year positions; the exit files' completeness sweep.
5. The opening balances for the new year — where the machinery carries year-to-date figures forward or opens fresh (mid-year go-lives in particular enter their opening earnings and tax figures so the annualised tax computes correctly from day one), the opening entries are made from documented figures and verified on the first new-year preview.

The new-year block.

6. The annual review round on its timetable (module 6) — commonly adjacent to year-end, scheduled so the round and the year-close do not collide on the same close week.
7. The settings walk (Chapter 2) and the control-register review (Chapter 3).
8. The annual confidentiality read (module 4) and the payroll access recertification's annual summary.

The year file. The year closes into one folder-of-folders: twelve run checklists and registers, twelve remittance evidence bundles, the certificates issued, the annual returns, the year's register closes, the settings and control pages as reviewed. Chapter 6's audit answers from this file; the operator's successor inherits it; the seven-year retention rule (the Accounts track's) governs its keeping.

Practical rule: the year-end block is scheduled in writing in month eleven — owners named per line, dates set clear of the December close's own pressure. A year-end improvised in the last week produces the one thing this track exists to prevent: numbers without documents, at the moment the most documents are due.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — The payroll audit
lessons.html:
Payroll is audited — by the external auditor's payroll section, by statutory inspections, by the owner's own review. This chapter is answering all three from one place.

What the auditor asks, mapped to what already exists.

1. "Show me that everyone paid exists and is approved." The run checklists' headcount reconciliations (every month's equation with its joiner/leaver names), the Employee records with their verification attachments, sampled assignments traced to their letters via the movement record. The ghost-employee question, answered by the controls that prevent it.
2. "Show me that pay matches its authority." Sampled slips traced: the base to the assignment to the letter; the variable lines to their Additional Salary records with evidence and approvals; the structural rates to the component register's rulings.
3. "Show me the statutory chain." Per sampled month: the register, its derived schedules, the Payment Entries, the receipts, the zero checks — module 2's evidence bundles, produced as filed. The slab against the law of its period; the certificates against the register's YTD.
4. "Show me the postings." The posting ties on the checklists; the wiring map; the cost-center trail from the Employee records to the branch P&L salary lines.
5. "Show me the exits." Sampled exit files: the settlement's two columns sourced, the signature, the balance closures, the tail schedules.
6. "Who can do what?" The payroll access list from the recertifications; the separations demonstrated (who prepared, who released — the names differ, every month).

The audit posture. Three rules for the visit:

1. Answer from the file, not from memory — every question above ends at a document, which is faster for the auditor and safer for the operator than any explanation.
2. The finding is a gift: an auditor's finding is a control gap found by a friendly reader on a schedule — it enters the incident log with its cause and produces its upstream fix exactly like an internal finding (the cause-read discipline, with an external trigger).
3. Never improve the past: the file presents as it was kept. A document "tidied" for the audit is worse than its original imperfection — the track's whole design is that the records were right when made, and the audit is where that design pays.

The internal audit rhythm. The owner's own review — quarterly or annual per the business's appetite — samples the same six questions at smaller scale, from the control register's map. The internal read's purpose is the external one's rehearsal and the finding found first: the gap the internal sweep catches in March is a process note; the same gap in the external audit is a finding with an audience.

Practical rule: after the first audit, file the auditor's request list with the year file — next year's preparation is this year's list, and a function that answers the list from the standing file in one sitting has passed the only structural test an audit really runs.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — Multi-company payroll and the handover test
lessons.html:
The track's last two structures: payroll across legal entities, and the proof that the function survives its operator.

Multi-company payroll. Where the site carries more than one company, payroll respects the legal separation completely — the Accounts track's rule, executed in payroll's terms:

1. Employment is per company: each Employee record belongs to its employing entity; a person genuinely serving two entities is two employment records or a documented cross-charge arrangement (the accountant's design), never one salary informally split.
2. The machinery is per company: Salary Components carry per-company account rows (module 1's Accounts table — the same component posting to each company's own chart); structures and slabs attach per company; the Payroll Entry runs per company (module 3's one-run rule reads: one run per company per period).
3. The statutory chain is per company: each entity's registrations, schedules, remittances, and certificates in its own name — the custody accounts per company's chart, the evidence bundles per company's file.
4. The registers split accordingly: the year files, the control register's evidence locations, and the audit answers all resolve per entity — the auditor of one company sees one company.

The handover test. The programme's standing structural test, applied to payroll: could a competent successor, given only the function's documentation, run next month's payroll correctly? The documentation the test reads is this track's artifact list — the settings record, the component register with rulings, the applicability page, the structures and the assignment register, the run checklist template and twelve filed examples, the remittance calendar and evidence bundles, the movement record, the variable-pay registers and policy pages, the exit checklist and files, the control register mapping all of it. The test is run for real:

1. The absence test: the backstop (a trained second — the accountant's payroll-literate colleague, or the deliberately cross-trained deputy) runs one full cycle on the documentation while the operator is on leave: the close, the run's five stations, the delivery, the remittance preparation. The operator answers no questions that the file should answer — and every question asked is a documentation finding, fixed on return.
2. The annual confirmation: the control register's review confirms the backstop's currency (procedures change; the backstop's training follows) and the documentation's completeness against the artifact list.

Why this is the certification's last word. A payroll that lives in one person's head holds the business hostage to leave, illness, and departure — and holds the operator hostage to their own indispensability. The track's every module built the alternative: pay computed by records, controlled by layers, evidenced in files, and documented to the standard a stranger can run. The operator who builds that has built the professional asset this certification names.

Practical rule: run the first absence test deliberately and soon — a planned week with the operator reachable — rather than discovering the documentation's gaps during an unplanned absence with the operator unreachable. The rehearsal is cheap; the emergency premiere is not.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Case study: HealthTrade's year close
lessons.html:
The structural chapters, executed. Every chapter appears.

The settings walk (Chapter 2). Run with the accountant in one sitting: the payroll basis confirmed as leave-based (matching the discipline the business actually keeps — attendance marking is branch-patchy, and the page says so honestly as the reason); holidays-in-working-days recorded with the worked example (the mid-month joiner computed both ways on the page); rounded totals confirmed against the bank file's behaviour; leave balances switched on for slips — the leave records having earned it through the HR-side cleanup; posting granularity confirmed consolidated, with the register-derivations note as the reason. Seven fields, seven one-line reasons, one page.

The control register (Chapter 3). Assembled from the modules' artifacts in an afternoon: nineteen controls, each with owner, cadence, and evidence location. The MD's oversight sampling begins the same quarter — two controls sampled unannounced, both evidenced in one lookup each.

A structural change through the lane (Chapter 4). The accountant's annual table update moves a statutory rate. The impact list names all three structures; the change enters at a period boundary — effective the 1st, entered before the close — previewed per structure with the plausibility check re-run, the batch verified both ways, and the first run's comparison matching the modelled movement to the naira. Staff are told before the slips tell them: one paragraph with the payday note.

The year-end (Chapter 5). Scheduled in writing in month eleven, owners named. The slab re-read confirms the current table; the applicability page re-confirms with one change — the threshold watch flags that the year's hiring has crossed a levy's headcount line, and the accountant registers the new obligation before its first due date rather than after its first penalty. The annual PAYE certificates issue to all staff from the closed registers; the employer's annual returns file from the same source; the year folder closes: twelve checklists, twelve bundles, the certificates, the returns, the register closes.

The audit (Chapter 6). The external auditor's payroll section visits in the new year. The six questions run from the control register's map: the headcount equations sampled across four months, three slips traced letter-to-slip, one remittance month walked register-to-receipt-to-zero, the driver's exit file read end to end (the signed settlement and repayment agreement answering the hard case's every question). One finding: two months' delivery logs missing their bounce-closure notes — logged, caused (the log line's template lacked the field), fixed upstream. The auditor's request list files with the year folder.

The handover test (Chapter 7). The deliberate absence: the operator takes a planned week mid-cycle; the trained backstop — the accounts assistant cross-trained across the quarter — runs the close, the five stations, the delivery, and the remittance preparation from the file. Two questions get asked; both become documentation fixes (the bank-file export's steps written down; the encashment rate basis's location noted on the exit checklist). The MD's year note: payroll ran for a week without its operator, answered an audit from one folder, and caught a new statutory obligation before it caught us — the function is now a system.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common mistakes & the track's eight laws
lessons.html:
The structural layer's recurring failures, the eighth law, and the track assembled.

Pattern 1 — the unexamined settings. Symptom: prorations nobody can explain; the holidays switch discovered mid-dispute; every slip computing on decisions nobody made. Cause: the Payroll Settings page never walked (Chapter 2). Fix: the walk with the accountant, the page's record — value, owner, date, reason — and the annual re-walk as the only change occasion.

Pattern 2 — the personal control set. Symptom: controls that exist as one person's habits; oversight that must ask where evidence lives; the audit as reconstruction. Cause: the controls never gathered (Chapter 3). Fix: the control register — every control with owner, cadence, evidence location — and the owner's unannounced sampling proving it real.

Pattern 3 — the mid-year drift. Symptom: a component's meaning silently changed in July; two halves of the year computing differently; history unreadable. Cause: structural changes without versioning (Chapter 4). Fix: new dated slabs, structure versions with batch assignments, successor components across boundaries, changes at period boundaries — history standing, always.

Pattern 4 — the improvised year-end. Symptom: certificates late, returns scrambled, the re-reads skipped in the December crush; the reform discovered by the first wrong run of January. Cause: no year calendar (Chapter 5). Fix: the year-end block scheduled in writing in month eleven, owners per line, clear of the close's own pressure.

Pattern 5 — the audit as performance. Symptom: the visit preceded by weeks of tidying; documents improved; answers from memory and charm. Cause: the file not kept audit-ready as a working state (Chapter 6). Fix: answer from the file as it was kept, findings as gifts into the cause read, and the request list filed for next year — the audit passing because the year did.

Pattern 6 — the indispensable operator. Symptom: payroll stops when one person is sick; the handover that would take months; the business hostage to a resignation. Cause: the function never structurally tested (Chapter 7). Fix: the artifact list complete, the backstop trained, the deliberate absence test run — and every question it surfaces fixed as the documentation finding it is.

The eighth law: payroll survives its operator — settings written, controls layered and registered, the machinery versioned, the year closed on its calendar, the audit answered from one folder, and the function proven by absence.

The track's eight laws.

1. Pay is computed by the records — components carry their accounts, structures the package, assignments the base, and every slip previews before it pays.
2. Statutory amounts are computed by components from the accountant's current table, posted to typed custody accounts, remitted by the calendar from the reserve, and zeroed every cycle.
3. The run is a procedure — records closed, drafts reconciled and read, posting tied before payment, payment separated from preparation, and the month closed on the checklist that proves it.
4. The slip is the employee's statement — computed by records, delivered one-to-one after the money moves, explained on request, and confidential everywhere else.
5. Variable pay enters as documents — approved before the close, computed from evidence, taxed by the flags and policy, and recovered only by written agreement on a self-ending schedule.
6. A pay change is a decision executed as a record — approved on the matrix, anchored to its letter, effective from its honest date, arrears by document, history standing.
7. The exit closes on documents — the final slip prorated, balances read day one, the settlement signed, the statutory tail carried, and access ending the same day.
8. Payroll survives its operator — settings written, controls layered, the year closed on its calendar, and the whole function answerable from one folder.

This completes the Payroll Professional track.
